The farm stand smelled of warm dirt and crushed leaves, and Emilie wiped strawberry juice off the counter for the third time that hour. Mr. Ruiz paid her five dollars a morning to stack baskets, make change, and answer questions, but today her math homework sat folded in her back pocket like a stone. She was supposed to draw two lines that crossed like an X and write about why strawberries cost two dollars a basket in June and six dollars in January. The lines themselves she could copy from the book, but she could not figure out who had first dreamed them up, and that question itched at her all morning.

A woman came by near noon, a recent refugee from Syria who had started coming every week with her two small sons. She counted coins carefully, and Emilie noticed she always bought more strawberries in summer, sometimes three baskets, and in winter she walked past them. "In winter they cost too much," the woman said simply, and Emilie felt something click, like a key finding its lock. More berries in summer made the price sink; fewer in winter made it climb. The X shape in her homework was just that idea, drawn.

During her break she asked Mr. Ruiz if she could borrow the shop's old laptop, its porous speaker crackling as it hummed to life. She typed "who made the supply and demand curves famous" and chewed her thumbnail while the page loaded. There it was. A British economist named Alfred Marshall had made the two crossing curves famous in his 1890 book, Principles of Economics. She read the name twice, then copied it onto her homework sheet in careful letters.

"Find what you needed?" Mr. Ruiz asked when she handed back the laptop.

"Alfred Marshall," Emilie said, holding up her paper. "He made my homework famous first." Outside, the strawberry vines flourished in the July heat, heavy with fruit, and she went back to the counter to stack another row of two-dollar baskets.

Matthew slouched at his table in room 12, staring at the photocopied page where Mr. Ruiz had typed the same question three times: What is the theme of the novel? Support your answer with a quotation. Last week Matthew had written "the theme is friendship" and gotten it back with a red circle around nothing, which felt worse than a circle around something wrong. At least a mistake could be diagnosed. This was just empty.

"You have to use the actual text," said Priya, leaning over. "Like, copy a line and connect it."

"I know that," Matthew said, though he did not. Their class novel was an old retelling of Romeo and Juliet, and half of it sounded like a foreign language. He flipped to his marked page and read aloud in a whisper: "'She hath not seen the change of fourteen years.'"

Priya squinted. "She hath not seen the change of fourteen years. What's hath?"

"Beats me. Maybe it's 'hates'?" He tried it. "She hates not seen the change of fourteen years." That collapsed instantly, like a tent with one pole missing. He read further and found "he doth keep the peace" and "what doth it profit a man." Doth kept showing up where a verb belonged. He tested a pattern, the way he tested cheat codes: swap doth for does. "He does keep the peace." That worked. He looked back at hath. If doth meant does, maybe hath meant has. "She has not seen the change of fourteen years." The whole sentence snapped into place.

"That's it," Priya said, writing it down. "So hath means has. That's, like, their word for it."

Matthew's hand shot up before he could talk himself out of it. When Mr. Ruiz called on him, he stood, ears hot, and read the quotation in both versions, the old words and the plain modern English underneath. "The theme is that kids grow up faster than the grown-ups want them to. She hasn't even turned fourteen yet, and the whole story is already happening to her."

Mr. Ruiz didn't smile, but he underlined something on his clipboard, and Priya kicked Matthew's chair leg under the table, twice, which was her way of cheering.

That night Matthew found his father's old copy of Shakespeare on the shelf at home, its cover soft from years of hands. He hadn't known why he'd avoided it before, and he didn't entirely know why he was opening it now, except that last week he'd looked at a page like this and seen a locked door, and today someone had handed him a key. The house smelled like burnt toast from the kitchen, and from downstairs his father called, "You reading that thing?"

"Yeah," Matthew said. "He doth write pretty good."

His father's laugh came through the floorboards.

Victor wanted his grandmother's annual art contest entry to be perfect, mostly because his cousin Priya had won it two years running. At the kitchen table in his grandparents' house, he kept drawing the same beach ball and it kept looking flat, like a sticker of a ball instead of a ball. His grandmother nurtureed his habit of trying again, sliding him a fresh peach and saying that she couldn't help him herself, since she had an allergy to pencils, which was her joke for arthritis. Grandpa, reading in the corner, looked over the top of his glasses and said one thing: "Artists call that line the terminator."

"Like the robot?" Victor said, but Grandpa only shrugged and went back to his book. Terminator. Robots didn't seem to have anything to do with a peach.

Then Victor carried the peach to the window, where the morning sun hit it sideways, and turned it slowly in his fingers. There was a line, curving around the fruit, where the bright gold stopped and the dusky side began. It wasn't a drawn line. Nothing marked it. It was simply the edge where the light stopped reaching, and on the table below, the peach threw a second, darker pool of shadow that stretched away from the sun. He fetched the desk lamp and angled it high, then low, watching the line slide and the cast shadow shorten and stretch like something alive. What if his ball looked flat because he had skipped that line entirely, shading everything softly the same way?

Back at the table, he sharpened his pencil to an acute point and drew the beach ball again, this time finding the terminator first, laying a definite shadow on the far side and a crisp cast shadow beneath it, then gently blending toward a bright spot where the lamp would have been. Grandpa wandered over, peach in hand, and studied the page. "Huh," he said. "Priya's going to hate this." Victor turned the drawing toward the window to check it in better light.

Paisley cracked the first egg into the bowl before she had measured anything else, and by nine thirty the counter looked like a flour bomb had gone off. "The muffins have to be out of the oven by eleven," her friend Ruby reminded her, "because Mr. Delgado, our upstairs tenant, comes down for coffee at eleven sharp, and he judges everything." Paisley raced to the pantry for baking powder, came back, and discovered she'd forgotten to preheat the oven entirely. "The oven's cold as a swimming pool," she groaned. Ruby peeked at the recipe card. "It says preheat first. Four hundred degrees. It also says something weird at the top."

The card read, in Grandma Cruz's handwriting: Mise en place. "It's French," Ruby said, squinting. "It means 'putting in place.' Measuring out every single ingredient before you start cooking." Paisley looked at her lumpy batter, then at the oven, then at the clock. Ten o'clock. If she kept hunting for cinnamon while things sat and oven temperatures climbed, nothing would be done by eleven, and Mr. Delgado would shake his head and call their kitchen impoverished, which was his word for anything missing blueberries.

"We start over," Paisley announced, dumping the batter into the sink with ceremony. "This time I test the French way." She turned the dial to four hundred, then lined up little bowls on the counter like soldiers: flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, oil, milk, one egg. Ruby rinsed blueberries and let them contribute to the cause by plopping them in a cup. "You look like a scientist," Ruby said. "I look like a person who knows where her cinnamon is," Paisley said, holding up the cinnamon like a trophy.

At eleven sharp the muffins came out golden, the tops cracked just right, and Mr. Delgado arrived downstairs sniffing the air like a bear at a picnic basket. He bit into one, chewed, and nodded slowly. "Not impoverished at all," he declared. "Who measured everything in advance?" Paisley raised her hand. "Mise en place," she said. "Second batch's on me," said Mr. Delgado, reaching for a second muffin.

Elena spread her battery, bulb, switch and coiled wire across the picnic table at the edge of the skate park, because her brother Tomas refused to skip practice and she refused to fail Monday's science demonstration. She clipped the wire to the battery, flipped the switch, and the bulb stayed dark. She unclipped and reclipped every connection, but it was like arguing with the ramp: the same input, the same nothing. The skaters had started to migrate to the shaded half-pipe as the tropical afternoon heat pressed down, and a plague of gnats circled her table, but she kept working.

She took the bulb off and clipped the wire straight to a small meter instead. If current was flowing, the needle would move even though she could not see current itself. It did not move. "So the battery's fine or it's not," she said to herself, "but something between here and here is broken." She tested each piece of wire by touching its ends to the meter until one stretch, cracked where skaters had rolled over it, gave nothing at all. She replaced it, flipped the switch, and the bulb glowed. When her friend Dara rolled up, Elena held the lit bulb and said, "It lights because the switch closes the path, so current goes around the whole loop through the filament."

A text arrived from Tomas, on the far ramp: "Coach says graph beats guessing. Did you try the meter trick or just stare at it?" Elena typed back: "Meter trick. Found a dead wire. Also took five readings of voltage and current with the good wire, like the handbook said."

She plotted the five points on graph paper, voltage up the side, current along the bottom. The points fell into a straight line, and when she extended it backward with her ruler, it passed through zero, where no voltage meant no current. The line climbed steeply, which matched the way her bulb pushed back against the flow. Dara leaned over her shoulder and read the page. "That line means something?" Elena tapped the slope with her pencil and said, "The slope is the resistance." Dara nodded slowly, spun her board up onto the table, and said, "Show me the bulb again."

Brielle had planned the whole week before Grandpa's suitcase even reached the porch. She would show him the rope swing, the vegetable garden, and the dilapidated shed at the back fence where her old bike still leaned against a broken shelf. But on the second morning, the kitchen filled with smoke from toast nobody noticed, and Grandpa just sat at the table reading his newspaper while the slices turned black.

"Grandpa, the toast!" Brielle grabbed the fork and flipped them off the burner before the smoke alarm could intervene. She waved a towel at the ceiling and studied him. Last summer, he had smelled her burning marshmallow from across the entire yard. She tested him quietly, saying nothing about the cinnamon rolls she had hidden in the oven to surprise him at lunch. When she finally brought them out, warm and fragrant enough to make her own mouth water, he thanked her politely, as if she had handed him a paper napkin.

That afternoon she ran a careful experiment in the backyard. She set out five cups on the picnic table: vanilla, lemon, coffee, onion, and plain water. "Tell me what each one is," she said, and Grandpa, who loved games, agreed at once. He identified the coffee, slowly, and guessed wrong on everything else. The plain water he called "soap." Brielle sat back on the bench, thinking about her grandmother, who had always known it was raining before anyone else because she could smell it coming, and who had once found a gas leak that no one else had noticed. Maybe she, too, had stopped being able to smell near the end, and maybe everyone had mistaken it for not paying attention. Brielle wondered whether she should have visited more that year instead of choosing soccer camp.

That evening she typed her notes into the library computer and found a word waiting for her: presbyosmia. "The sense of smell naturally declines in old age," the screen said, "a change called presbyosmia." She read it twice, then printed it.

On the last day of his visit, Grandpa stood by the grill in the backyard while Brielle watched the hamburgers for him, flipping each one at exactly the right moment. He talked about his own grandfather's kitchen, and the bread that always seemed to come out of the oven a little too dark. "We teased him about it for years," he said, shaking his head. "Now I wonder."

"I'll be your nose while you're here," Brielle said, and handed him the spatula so he could do the honors himself.

Anthony's problem was simple: someone had logged into his library account three times overnight and held every copy of the new space graphic novel until June. He had never told anyone his password, which was anthony123. In computer class that morning, Ms. Ruiz put a challenge on the board: create a password, then explain in one sentence why reusing it everywhere is a bad idea.

He typed anthony123 into the practice box, and a bar glowed red. Weak. He tried Anthony!2013! and the bar turned yellow, then green when he added the name of his eccentric neighbor's dog, Rickets, who wore a raincoat even in July. "A strong password has length, weird capital letters, and symbols," Anthony said to his partner, Divya. "So why can't I use the same strong one for everything?"

"Because if one site leaks it, they get all of you," Divya said. "Like a decomposer. One fungus gets into a fallen log, and the whole log goes." Anthony thought about the library account. Whoever guessed anthony123 might now try it on his game account too, since he had used it there since second grade. He tested it: he typed anthony123 into a fake login the class had set up, and the screen showed exactly which of his other pretend accounts would fall. All of them did.

That afternoon the class debated something Divya had found while researching: search engines. "In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results," she read, "or they risk deceiving users." A boy named Marcus argued that ads dressed up as regular results were fair game. "No," Anthony said. "If you can't tell what's paid and what's natural, they violate the rule. It's like a password that looks strong but isn't." The class voted, and Marcus switched sides. Anthony copied his new password onto a scrap of paper, folded it twice, and tucked it deep in his backpack.

Anthony raised his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "Mr. Ruiz, why does my voice do that croaky thing now?" It had happened that morning in the shower, mid-song, and again at lunch when he'd yelled for the basketball. Mr. Ruiz only grinned and said, "Ask the choir teacher. That's her frontier, not mine." Frontier, Anthony thought. Like his voice was wild, unclaimed land.

Flashback: last spring, in this same room, Anthony had sung the solo in the spring assembly without a single wobble. His voice had been light and steady, and his grandmother had recorded the whole thing on her phone. Now, three months into seventh grade, he had signed up to audition for the winter concert, and the audition was Friday. He wanted that solo more than he'd wanted anything since the new skate park opened.

So he ran an experiment. He borrowed a notebook and made a tally: every time his voice cracked, he wrote down the note he'd been trying to hit. In the shower he sang up a scale. Low notes: smooth. Middle notes: fine. High notes: crack, crack, crack. There was a distinct breaking zone, like a fence across his range. He tried warming up first, then drinking cold water, then not talking all day. Nothing moved the fence. Whatever was happening was happening on its own, invisibly, somewhere inside.

On Thursday he brought his notebook to choir practice and showed the tallies to Ms. Park. "It's the larynx," she said simply. "It grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, so the voice may crack while this happens." Anthony stared at his tally marks. Longer and thicker. It wasn't a fence at all; it was construction. His voice was being rebuilt, bigger.

That night he wrote a note and left it on the kitchen counter for his dad, who worked late.

Dad, I audition tomorrow. Don't be intimidated by any weird sounds from the music room, it's just my larynx renovating. Wish me luck. Anthony.

At the audition Friday, Anthony chose a lower song than the one he'd sung in spring. He reached the highest note of the new arrangement, felt a small tremor pass through like a truck on a distant road, and kept going. Ms. Park circled his name. "Solo," she said. "Second verse, low key."

Anthony punched the air so hard his pencil flew across the music room and rolled under the piano.

Scarlett held the tuning fork against her knee, struck it, and listened until the hum faded to nothing. The music room smelled like rosin and old radiator dust, and Mr. Petra's note on the board said only: A above middle C, 440. Find it yourself. She plucked the A string on her violin. The two sounds wobbled against each other, a sour beating she could feel in her teeth even though she couldn't see it. Something hidden was making that wobble, and she suspected it was the string being slightly too low. She turned the fine tuner a hair, plucked again. The wobble slowed. Another hair. The wobble almost vanished, and when it did, the note felt round and steady, like two waves lying exactly on top of each other. She tuned the other strings from that A, matching each one to its neighbor, guessing and correcting.

Behind her, Dex was hammering the drum set at full blast, then dropping to silence, then blasting again. He wanted the drum solo in the spring concert more than he wanted lunch, and he'd been practicing like a startled thundercloud all week.

"That's not a crescendo," Scarlett said. "A crescendo means gradually getting louder. You're doing it all at once, like a door slamming."

Dex narrowed his eyes. "So what's the opposite called?"

"Decrescendo. Or diminuendo. It means gradually getting softer." She remembered her own first rehearsal in September, when she'd slammed into a loud passage and the whole violin section had flinched, and she still wasn't sure whether the look Mr. Petra had given her was amusement or disappointment. Probably both. "Watch."

She played a scale that grew from a whisper to a swell, then shrank back down like a tide going out. Dex copied her on the drums, rolling louder by careful degrees until the windows seemed to hum, then easing off until the sound deteriorated into a faint patter like distant rain.

"That analysis of yours," Dex said, "is annoyingly correct." He tapped the rim of the snare, a brittle little tick in the quiet room, and grinned. "Again, from the top. You count us in."

Scarlett lifted her bow and said, "One, two, three, four."

Samantha spread the giant world map across two airport chairs, which was against the rules of airports everywhere, probably, and made her brother Marcus climb over her feet to get to the window seat he had been guarding since check-in. Their flight to Santiago left in two hours, and Dad had given her a mission: figure out exactly where they were going, using only the map and the strange squiggling lines all over it.

"Those are latitude and longitude," Marcus said, without looking away from the window. "Dad told you that already. Twice."

"I know what they're called," Samantha said. "What I don't know is how they work. There's a difference." She traced a finger along a horizontal line labeled 20 and then a vertical one labeled 70. Somewhere they crossed, if the lines meant anything at all, was Chile. She found Santiago, then put her finger near a pale orange patch to the north and squinted at the tiny label. Atacama Desert.

Marcus leaned over, chewing a granola bar he'd been rationing since security like it was the last one on Earth. "What are you doing now?"

"I made a climate graph last week for school, for that desert," Samantha said. "Everybody else's graph had little bars for every month's rain. Half of mine was just empty space. I thought I messed up." She frowned at the map, then at the scribbled note in her notebook from the research: some weather stations there have never recorded rain. Not a little rain. Not rare rain. Never. "I spent an hour checking my math."

Marcus laughed so hard he almost lost his granola bar out the side of his mouth. "So your graph was right and the desert is just broken?"

"The desert isn't broken, it's just the driest place." She tapped the crossing point of her two lines. "See, 20 across, 70 down, give or take. That's how you say where a city is. Dad says pilots use numbers like that for everything." She wrote "20 S, 70 W, Atacama, zero rain ever" and underlined it twice, then drew a small triumphant camel in the margin, even though camels definitely did not flourish there. She doubted many organisms did, actually, in a place with no rain at all.

Marcus peered at her notebook. "Can I draw the camel a hat? Camels look versatile, they could pull off a hat."

Samantha handed him the pencil just as the gate agent called their row, and the two of them folded the map into a lopsided square and ran.

Parker scanned the field from the third deck, popcorn warm in his lap, and counted jerseys. His uncle had budgeted exactly enough cash for two hot dogs and one souvenir each, so Parker had chosen the popcorn to make his money last. He counted again, because the first count had to be wrong. "Maya, what numbers do you see out there?" he asked his cousin. She squinted through the railing. "Seventeen, thirty-one, six, nine, eleven." Parker checked the scoreboard roster. Every player had a number, and every number was there, except one. Nobody on either team wore 42. He wondered if 42 was bad luck, or against some rule nobody had told him.

Then the whole stadium went weird. The public address announcer said it was a special ceremony before the first pitch, and every single player on both teams jogged out wearing the same jersey, all with 42 on the back. "Why is everyone dressed the same?" Maya asked, tugging Parker's sleeve. "Did they lose their laundry?" Parker didn't laugh, because he was too busy thinking. Same number on every player, on every team, at the same time. That wasn't a coincidence. That looked like something people did on purpose, together, for one number.

The woman in the next seat, there with her grandson, leaned over. "You two look puzzled." She held up her grandson's tiny foam finger, which also had a 42 on it. Maya pointed at the field. "Why does everybody have that number?" The woman smiled. "In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete was honored that way." Parker whispered the words to himself so he would remember them. Retired, for every team. Not just one club, all of them. That was why he had never seen a 42 in any game he had watched on TV, not once. He had thought it was chance. It was the opposite of chance.

His uncle came back from the concession stand and handed Maya her hot dog before she even had to ask, because he always noticed who was waiting. Parker pointed at the field. "Uncle Theo, look. Every team in baseball gave up number 42 so one man could keep it forever." His uncle sat down slowly, looked at all those matching jerseys glowing under the lights, and put his cap over his heart. "Then let's stand up," he said. "All of us."

Julia slid her coordinate grid across the table until it bumped Mr. Okoye's tray of colored pencils, and the smell of sharpened wood drifted up as Marcus grabbed two and tossed her the green one. Math club met in the cafeteria every Tuesday, and today the whiteboard read "Two-Step Equations: y = 2x + 1." Julia's problem was y = 2x + 3, and she needed two points so she could draw the line. She picked x = 1 first, because one was easy, and got y = 5. Then she wanted x = one half, just to see what would happen.

"When x is one half, I get two times one half plus three," she said, talking it through. "So that's one plus three. Four." She plotted (1, 5) and then moved carefully to the halfway point between 0 and 1 on the x-axis, and up four. Marcus leaned over, chewing the eraser end of his pencil, which Julia could perceive was his thinking habit, because he only did it when a problem had him stuck.

"I wanted x = one third," Marcus said. "But then y equals two thirds plus three, and I can't add those." He scribbled, crossed out, scribbled again. "So I multiplied the denominators instead. Three times one is three, and I turned three into three over one, so three times one gives me three over one." He frowned at his paper. "Two thirds plus nine thirds is eleven thirds. It works, but it's ugly."

Julia tried it herself with different numbers, using the flat side of her ruler as a straightedge and making a quick adaptation to her method: instead of guessing, she multiplied the denominators every time. Each answer came out correct, and each time the fraction was bigger than it needed to be, waiting to be simplified. "It always works," she said slowly. "Multiplying the denominators gives you a common denominator. Just not always the smallest one."

"So it's like a shortcut that costs you later," Marcus said. "You get there, then you have to clean up."

Julia drew her line through both points, checked it against Marcus's paper, and pressed the green pencil down hard where the two lines crossed. "Same line," she said. "Different roads."

Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it top to bottom twice, the way his older sister Priya had told him to. Preheat the oven to 375. Grease the muffin pan. Stir the wet ingredients and the dry ones in separate bowls, then fold them together. He twisted the oven dial and waited for the preheat light, feeling like he had finally been trusted with something real, because Priya had promised he could bake these blueberry muffins entirely on his own while she worked on her own project: the pasta sauce simmering on the back burner, which she was determined to make thick enough to cling to a spoon.

While the bowls came together, Nolan measured the flour carefully, level with the back of a knife. Last winter, he remembered, he had tried pancakes without measuring anything, and the batter had rebelled by turning into a gluey lump that refused to flatten even in the pan. Priya had laughed until she couldn't breathe, and then she had shown him how to scoop flour lightly and sweep the cup clean. "That's why recipes exist," she had said. He wasn't going to make that mistake again, and besides, the muffins were his proof that he could feed himself something that wasn't toast.

Priya lifted the lid off her sauce and frowned. "It's still soupy. It's been twenty minutes." She stirred it and sighed toward the window. Nolan glanced over while spooning batter into the pan, and something clicked. The lid had been clamped on the whole time. "Try it with the lid off," he said. She gave him a look. "Steam can't get out with the lid on," he said. "Try it and see."

She propped the lid against the sugar jar and let the sauce bubble uncovered. By the time his muffins had risen into golden domes and he was sliding the pan onto the rack, her sauce had gone from watery to thick enough to coat the wooden spoon. "Hey, it worked," she said, dipping the spoon and tilting it slowly. "Ours both worked." Nolan pulled the oven mitt, the one with the frail thumb worn almost through, onto his hand and opened the door. "Careful," Priya said. "Hot." He lifted the pan out and set it on the rack, and the smell of blueberries filled the whole kitchen.

Christopher sat on Marcus's floor with the phone box in his lap, because tomorrow was the big day and Marcus's dad had picked the phone up early so they could set it together. The plan had one catch, and Christopher had read it four times: two gigabytes of data a month, and that was all. He wanted to know what actually ate the data, since you couldn't watch it disappear.

"It's the videos," Marcus said. "Obviously."

"But Grandpa sends me videos of geese and they barely count," Christopher said. He remembered last fall, when Grandpa texted him a clip of a big migratory flock passing over the lake, and the data meter barely moved. That was the clue. So he borrowed Marcus's phone and ran a test: he played one video with the wifi off and wrote down the number, then played the same video on wifi and checked again. The wifi number stayed flat. It wasn't videos that used data. It was videos without wifi. The hidden rule showed itself, and Christopher felt like he'd pulled a curtain back.

"My dad says there's a poster at the store," Marcus said, pulling up a picture on his tablet. "It's supposed to depict the very first handheld cellular call ever made. Some Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper made it right on a New York street on April 3, 1973."

"Fifty years before phones like this," Christopher said, holding up the slim box. "Pocket phones are older than my parents."

Marcus read a message out loud that his sister had sent from the store: "Kid in front of me asked how long people have carried phones around. Manager said 1973. Kid said, 'That's it?' and everyone laughed."

Christopher texted his dad: I figured out the data. Wifi at home for videos. Regular stuff is fine anywhere. Dad sent back one word: "Deal."

Christopher slid the phone under his pillow like a buried treasure and set his alarm for tomorrow.

The tent smelled like pine and cold canvas when Lily unzipped her bag the first night in the park. She set her toothpaste, her sunscreen, and a half-eaten bag of trail mix in the corner by her sleeping pad, the way she did at home. Outside, her dad was hauling the cooler from the car to the metal bear locker by the picnic table, and her mom was being optimistic about the clouds breaking up before morning. Lily could hear the whole camp settling down, quiet except for a creek somewhere behind the trees.

At breakfast the next day, a ranger walked through the loop checking lockers. She stopped at their site and looked at the picnic table, then at the tent. "Everything with a scent needs to go in the locker overnight," she said. "In Yosemite and parks like it, anything scented counts as food. That includes toothpaste, sunscreen, and trash." Lily's dad thanked her, and the ranger moved on to the next campsite.

Lily sat with her granola bar halfway to her mouth and thought about that. Toothpaste counted as food? It was minty, not edible, at least not on purpose. She tried to imagine a bear caring about sunscreen. The rule seemed strange until she considered how a bear searches, not with its eyes but with its nose, and a nose did not sort things the way a grocery store did. If it smelled like something, it was something.

That evening she offered to transport the last load to the locker herself. She packed the toothpaste, the sunscreen, and the empty wrapper from her dad's sandwich, and she counted the items as she placed them inside, one by one, keeping her own little economy of scents, everything tallied, nothing left over. She zipped the tent empty and walked back under a sky going dark and blue.

"Did we get everything?" her mom called from the fire.

"Every single thing with a smell," Lily said. "The tent is clean."

Elliot pushed his peas around his plate while his sister Maya talked and talked. She played forward on the Riverside Ravens, and tonight she had news.

"Guess who has the best shooting percentage in the whole league," Maya said, grinning across the tranquil kitchen. "Me. One hundred percent. The website says so."

Dad raised his eyebrows. "Better than Kelsey Okafor?"

"Better than everybody."

Elliot set down his fork. Kelsey Okafor had scored nineteen goals this season; he'd watched her slot three in one game from the bleachers, hugging his jacket around himself because the wind off the field cut right through it, nothing to insulate him but that thin jacket. He tried to remember Maya ever taking a shot. He pictured game after game, her passing, passing, passing, always looking for the open teammate. He could not recall a single shot.

"How many shots have you actually taken?" he asked.

Maya's grin flickered, just for a second. "That doesn't matter. A percentage is a percentage."

Elliot went and got the laptop from the hall. The league site listed every player, ranked by shooting percentage, and Maya sat at the top with 1 for 1, one hundred percent. Kelsey sat seventh with 46 for 61, which worked out to seventy-five percent. From one perspective the ranking looked like the whole truth. Elliot scrolled and counted the shots column again, just to be sure. One shot. Maya had taken one shot all season.

"You made one out of one," he said slowly. "If you'd taken that one shot in the first game and never played again, you'd still be perfect."

Maya stabbed a meatball. "I'm still ranked first."

"Ranked first on one shot." He turned the laptop toward her. "Kelsey made forty-six. She just missed some too."

Dad leaned over to look, and Maya stared at the two numbers side by side, her finger hovering over the screen. Finally she laughed, a short surprised sound.

"Fine," she said. "Saturday, I'm taking at least five shots."

Naomi stood at the door of the community hall holding a box of dates she had bought with her allowance. Her best friend Samir had invited her to come along with his family, and she had one morning to figure out a puzzle. Last night, when she asked what gift to bring, Samir had said, "Bring dates," but the ones at the store came in three sizes, and she had guessed the small box, because everyone at the hall would surely be saving their appetite for later.

Inside, the long tables were already crowded with plates of samosas, sweet sev, and a mountain of sheer khurma. Samir's grandmother pressed a warm bowl of it into Naomi's hands. Naomi took one bite, then stopped. "Wait," she said to Samir. "Aren't you still fasting until sunset? Should you cease eating right now?"

Samir laughed so hard he nearly dropped his plate. "It's Eid al-Fitr," he said. "That's the celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month when we fast from dawn until sunset. Nobody's fasting today. That's the whole point."

Naomi felt her face go warm. She looked down at the small box of dates in her bag. She had spent nine dollars on it, expecting a crowd of hungry people who would not touch food until dark. Now she could see dozens of families eating and laughing at ten in the morning, and her gift looked tiny. The gift table stood near the stage, and the volunteers would carry everything to the kitchen at noon, when the games began. She had two hours.

She tried to think of it from Samir's perspective. A month of no food or water between dawn and sunset, and then one morning of feasting. Of course everyone wanted to eat now, all at once, all together. That was the pattern she had missed. So what did a hall full of people who had just finished a month of fasting actually need? She remembered the water station by the entrance, where a line of kids waited for paper cups.

Naomi walked to the kitchen and found a volunteer stacking trays. "Could I trade this box of dates for a job?" she asked. "I could refill the water cups. There's a long line." The volunteer, an uncle with a whiskered smile, said that refilling was the most controversial job in the hall, because last year two boys had argued over who got to hold the pitcher, and he had decided girls poured better. He handed her the big blue pitcher.

For the next hour Naomi carried water to every table, and children cheered each time the pitcher arrived, and Samir's grandmother saved her a second bowl of sheer khurma, this time with extra nuts. When the volunteers finally cleared the gift table, the small box of dates sat alone on the corner, and Samir's little sister grabbed it, tore it open, and announced, "Dates! I get the first one."

The bean plant by the window had drooped overnight, and Alexis had ten minutes before the bell to figure out why. Her lab partner, Marcus, leaned over the pot and said, "That plant is ugly. It's the worst one in the room." Alexis frowned. "That doesn't help. I think somebody forgot to water it, and that's a claim we can actually test." Marcus shrugged. "It's my opinion. You can't prove an opinion wrong." Alexis stopped, spoonful of gravel for drainage in hand, because that sentence was exactly what her older brother had shouted at dinner last night before their mom made them both go to bed.

She scrutinize every part of the setup. The soil was dry and pulling away from the sides of the pot, so the plant had not been watered, that much was certain. But the control plant two tables over had also been skipped and it looked fine. So lack of water alone could not be the whole answer. Marcus tapped the window glass. "This one gets cooked by the sun all afternoon. That window is like a toaster." Alexis checked the blinds, which hung half open, and then felt the leaves. Warm, almost hot. Her reasoning went like this: dry soil plus hot leaves, versus dry soil and cool leaves across the room. The difference was the window.

"We water both plants the same amount," she said, pulling the blinds down on their side only, "and see which one perks up by tomorrow." Marcus wrote it on a sticky note and slapped it on the pot like a tiny flag. When Ms. Ortiz walked past, she raised an eyebrow at the flag, and Marcus pointed at Alexis. "Her experiment. I'm the official note writer. It comes with benefits." Ms. Ortiz moved on, but Alexis noticed she turned down the radiator near their table on her way, which had to mean something.

The classroom grew tranquil as the last students packed up. Alexis snapped a photo of the droopy plant so tomorrow they would have proof, not just a memory of it. On her way out she grabbed the watering can and topped off the control plant too, because fair tests deserved fair treatment. "Tomorrow," Marcus said at the door, holding it open for her, "we find out if I'm wrong." Alexis grinned. "You're wrong about the ugly part either way. That bean plant is my favorite one in the room, and nobody can test me on that."

Dad had promised to teach her something on this trip, and by the second morning he still hadn't, so Lily took matters into her own hands. She spread the topographic map of the park across the picnic table, weighed its corners down with pinecones, and frowned at it until Marcus, her little brother, leaned over her shoulder.

"What are you doing?"

"Finding us." She traced her finger along the thin curved lines that looped around a brown blob near the middle of the map. She knew from school that the numbered lines running up and down and side to side were latitude and longitude, and that the town of Fairview sat where two of them crossed. If she could read those numbers, she could tell anyone on Earth exactly where Fairview was. But first she wanted to know how tall the hill above their campsite was, because Dad had bet her a marshmallow that she couldn't figure it out. She counted four lines from the bottom of the hill to the top and multiplied. Two hundred feet per line meant eight hundred feet, which seemed too steep for a hill that had taken them only twenty minutes to climb.

Marcus poked the tiny print along the map's bottom edge. "What's this little box say?"

Lily bent closer. The legend, small enough that she'd walked right past it, said the contour interval was forty feet. "The contour interval," she read slowly. That meant the difference in height between one contour line and the next was forty feet. She redid her count, and the hill came out at one hundred sixty feet, which felt about right for their burning calves and one rest stop. Her first answer had implied the hill was five times taller than it was. She thought about last summer, when she'd guessed the lake was a mile across and refused to check, and Dad had rowed her across it in twenty minutes without saying a word.

"So the hill's smaller than you thought," Marcus said.

"It's exactly the right size. I was the wrong size." She found Fairview's crossing lines, copied the numbers onto her hand, and held it up. "Thirty-four point six north, ninety-eight point two west. Now I can find anything."

"Even the bathroom?"

"Especially the bathroom," Lily said, and folded the map into her back pocket.

The washing machine at home had died on Tuesday, so on Saturday Mya and her dad carried three baskets of laundry to the Spin Cycle Laundromat, which smelled like warm soap and pennies. Her dad dropped the baskets, fed quarters into two machines, and then handed her a five dollar bill and a short list written on a dryer sheet. "Milk and stamps," he said. "The corner store. You know the way."

She knew the way. She had walked it maybe two hundred times, but always with somebody. The light at Foster Street took forever to change, and the store's bell jangled when the door moved even a centimeter, so you could hear customers coming before you saw them. Still, standing at the laundromat door with the bill folded in her fist, she felt hesitant, like the sidewalk outside had gotten longer since the last time she'd looked at it.

"Your mother walked to that store alone at nine," her dad said, which was supposed to be encouraging but wasn't. Mya thought about her mom at nine, small and fearless, and decided she could manage at twelve. She walked out. At the corner store she found the milk, stood in line, and counted her change twice at the register because the cashier had already turned to the next customer. Two dollars and thirty-one cents. She counted it again on the walk back, lips moving, and it came out the same both times, which felt like passing a secret test nobody had announced.

Back at the laundromat, the first load had finished, and Mya pulled out her white school shirt and winced. It was pink. Not pink like a sunset, pink like a watermelon that had lost an argument. Her dad held it up and said, "Well." In the load there was also one red sock, brand new, that her little brother had insisted needed washing before Monday.

Mya laid the shirt flat on the folding table and stared at it. She hadn't mixed the clothes up; her brother had dropped the sock into the whites basket himself. But something had to have traveled from the sock to the shirt, because the sock had come out barely lighter than it went in, and the shirt had gone in white and come out pink. She thought about the water, how it had sat in the machine with all of it tumbling together for half an hour, and she said, "The new sock let dye go into the wash water, and the water carried it to everything pale in there." Her dad said, "That's why people sort by colour, kid," and she thought, nobody ever tells you why, they just say sort.

She ran a test with the second load, which was her idea. Darks in one machine, whites and pale things alone in another, no new red anything. When that load came out, everything was the color it was supposed to be, and she folded it in stacks, smug, while her dad watched his phone.

Later, walking home with the milk, she turned the pink shirt over in the bag and thought about her brother's sock, which was technically his fault but mostly just a sock doing what new red socks do. She hadn't checked the basket before starting the load, either. She still wasn't sure whose job that was.

"I'm wearing it anyway," her brother announced at dinner. "Pink's my color."

Alexis stood at the zucchini booth at the farmers' market, holding a recipe card her grandmother had written out in loopy blue ink: Zucchini Honey Muffins, makes twelve. "One dollar each," said the farmer, "or three for two." Alexis counted her coins and picked three, choosing the ones that were small and heavy, the way Gran had taught her last summer.

She could still remember that day clearly. Gran had let her measure the flour all by herself, and Alexis had been so proud that she'd declared the kitchen a monarchy with herself as queen. "Then I hereby classify you as the royal taste tester," Gran had said, bowing so low her reading glasses slid off. They had laughed until the muffins almost burned.

Today was different, though, because Alexis was baking alone. Gran was at the dentist, and the kitchen was Alexis's whole responsibility. She grated the zucchini, cracked the eggs, and stirred until her arm ached. The recipe card said, in Gran's handwriting at the bottom: Preheat oven to 375. Don't skip this. Alexis looked at the oven. The oven looked back, cold and blank. The last time she'd baked with Gran, she remembered, the muffins had come out pale and squat, dense as hockey pucks. Gran had frowned at them and said, "Hmm. What did we do differently?" Alexis hadn't known then.

She thought about it now, turning the wooden spoon in the batter. Gran always put the tray in after the oven had beeped. Alexis, that day, had slid the tray in right away to save time, because waiting was boring. The pale, squat muffins had gone in before the oven was hot. She had never connected those two things until this moment, standing alone in the kitchen with the oven still cold. So that was what preheating meant: waiting until the oven reached the temperature you set before the batter went in, so baking started at the right heat. She turned the dial and sat on the counter to wait, swinging her sneakers against the cupboard.

The wait felt endless, so she cut the last zucchini into diagonal slices and arranged them on the counter like a tiny green fence. When the oven finally beeped, she filled the paper liners, slid the tray in, and set the timer for twenty-two minutes exactly.

The muffins rose into golden domes, crackled on top, and smelled like honey and Sunday morning. She carried them, still warm, to the farmers' market in a basket covered with a dish towel. The zucchini farmer took one bite and closed his eyes. "Your gran's recipe?"

"Mine," Alexis said. "Baked by the queen herself."

He bowed so low his cap fell off. "Then I hereby classify myself as the royal taste tester."

"Get in line," Alexis said, and lifted the towel.

Harrison stood in the kitchen holding his speech cards like they might bite. Tomorrow he had to give a two-minute speech in front of the whole class, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and every time he practiced, he sped up until the words crashed into each other like dominoes.

"Again," said his sister Priya, munching a granola bar at the table. "You just said your hook and your first point in one breath."

"I know." Harrison dropped into a chair. "I can't figure out where to stop."

Priya shoved her laptop toward him. On the screen was a script from her school play, covered in pencil slashes. "Watch," she said, and pointed at one. "Actors split a script into beats," she said. "A new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift." She tapped a slash between two lines. "My thought changes there, so I stop. New thought, new beat."

Harrison grabbed a pencil. That was the hidden rule he'd been missing. His speech wasn't one long river of words; it was chunks, and each chunk had a job. He spread his cards on the table and hunted for the places where his thinking changed. After the hook, slash. After point one, slash. He marked all of them, then added one more and excluded the part about his uncle's failed business, because it didn't fit any of his three points no matter how much he liked it.

"Ready?" Priya set the kitchen timer for two minutes.

He stood up, took a breath, and started. "What if I told you a lemonade stand could pay for a new bike?" Pause. "That's income, money coming in." Pause. At every slash he stopped, and the stops made the next sentence land harder. Priya grinned so wide her grin looked infectious, and Harrison caught it.

The timer buzzed. One minute fifty-eight.

"You sounded like a person," Priya announced, "not a panicking vacuum cleaner."

Harrison squared his cards. "One more time."

Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table and stared at the blank page. Tomorrow she had to draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. Her motivation was simple: Mrs. Okafor had promised the best diagram would hang in the hallway for the whole school year, and Elena wanted that wall more than anything.

She had just drawn a fat yellow sun when her little brother Theo came out carrying their grandfather's old microscope and two mystery slides. "Grandpa said one is leaf and one is cheek cells," Theo said, setting them down beside her crayons. "But he forgot which is which. Can we look?"

Elena cherished afternoons like this, when a problem just appeared out of nowhere. She clipped the first slide under the lens and leaned down. The cells were neat little rectangles, like bricks in a wall, lined up in tidy rows. She switched to the second slide and squinted. These cells were blobby, roundish, scattered every which way like spilled beads.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Plant cells have rigid walls, so they're fixed and boxy, like these bricks. Animal cells only have a flexible membrane, so they come out rounded and irregular." She tapped the first slide. "Leaf. And the blobby ones are from somebody's cheek." Theo made a face. "Grandpa's cheek," Elena said, and they both laughed.

Then she stopped laughing, because something clicked. She pulled the leaf slide out and looked at her poster. "Theo, that's the whole point of my food chain," she said, grabbing a green crayon. "The sun feeds the leaf, and the leaf is made of those boxy little bricks, millions of them. A caterpillar eats the nutritious leaves and gets fat, a robin eats the caterpillar, and a hawk eats the robin. Sun, leaf, caterpillar, robin, hawk." She drew arrows down the page. "Every link is feeding the next one."

"But what if one link disappears?" Theo asked, peeling an orange and handing her half without being asked, because he could see she was on a roll and wouldn't stop to eat.

"Let's find out," Elena said. She drew a second chain, then scribbled the caterpillars out entirely. "No caterpillars means the robins go hungry and leave. Then the hawks lose their food too, and there are way too many leaves with nobody eating them." She sat back. "One missing link, and the whole chain gets weird."

Theo held up the leaf slide to the light. "So these little boxes feed everything?"

"These little boxes feed everything," Elena said, and drew an extra-large leaf right next to the sun.

Camille pushed her noodles around her plate and stared at the flyer propped against the salt shaker. Saturday's neighborhood garage sale started at eight, and Mrs. Okafor's telescope, the one Camille had wanted all summer, would be gone by nine if she didn't figure out a plan. Her brother Theo slurped his milk and grinned.

"You still moping about that telescope? It's just a tube with mirrors."

"It's not just anything," Camille said. "It's the only one on the whole street. And I only have eleven dollars."

Dad set down his fork. "Eleven dollars for a telescope? She'll want thirty, maybe more."

"Then I'll never get it," Camille said, and her stomach felt tight and cold. But then she remembered something. At the spring sale, Mrs. Okafor had stacked contemporary mystery novels, glossy and new-looking, and priced them at five dollars each. Nobody bought a single one. By eleven she had dropped them to a dollar, and by noon the whole stack was gone. The old battered paperbacks, though, priced at a quarter from the start, had sold out in an hour.

Camille sat up straight. "It depends on how many people want it and how many there are," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "If a lot of buyers want something and there's only one, the price goes up. If there's a pile and few takers, the price has to come down until everything sells." She grabbed Theo's napkin and scribbled numbers. "So I'll wait. If nobody else wants the telescope, she might lower the price before noon."

"That's a gamble," Dad said. "Someone else might grab it."

Camille's motive wasn't greed, she told herself; it was math. Saturday morning she hovered near the telescope, hands sweating, while Mrs. Okafor called out lower and lower prices. Ten o'clock: twenty dollars. Eleven: fifteen. At eleven forty, a boy picked it up, and Camille's heart contracted with fear. He put it down and wandered off.

"Twelve dollars," Mrs. Okafor announced, checking her watch. "Sale closes at noon."

Camille held up her eleven dollars and her lucky quarter. "Eleven twenty-five?"

Mrs. Okafor laughed. "Sold. You know, when what buyers want matches what sellers have left, that's the market-clearing price. You found mine."

Camille hugged the telescope all the way home.

The morning bus smelled like wet boots and orange peel, and Marcus would not stop talking. "My cousin says the new stadium tax is going to cost every family in town two thousand dollars a year," he announced to the whole back row. "He saw it in an ad. It had graphs."

Gabrielle pulled her backpack onto her lap. Two thousand dollars sounded like a lot, but it also sounded like the kind of number somebody might have invented. Marcus's cousin, last month, had claimed the school was canceling summer, and before that, that the lake fish were all dying from a spill nobody else had heard of. Gabrielle had begun to notice a pattern: the cousin's statements came in two flavors. Some were just opinions, like "the stadium is ugly," which nobody could check. Others were statements about the world, like "two thousand dollars per family," which either matched reality or didn't.

"Is two thousand dollars something you can verify?" she asked.

"What does verify mean?" said Priya from across the aisle. Priya wanted to be class president and had been collecting opinions all week, writing them in a spiral notebook titled WHAT THE PEOPLE WANT. "Because if the people believe the tax is two thousand dollars, that's what matters."

"No," Gabrielle said. "Believing isn't the same as it being true. My mom calls statements like that claims. A claim you can look up. An opinion you can only agree or disagree with." She paraphrased it another way, since Priya was still frowning. "If I say the bus smells like oranges, that's an opinion. If I say we're getting oranges every Tuesday, you could check."

Marcus said his cousin was never wrong. Priya said her notebook had eleven entries against the tax already. The bus lurched around the corner by the pharmacy, where a sign in the window advertised free delivery on prescriptions, and Gabrielle made a plan.

That night she and her dad had watched a TV ad about the stadium, and afterward her dad had looked it up on his phone. "PolitiFact," he'd said. "A fact-checking website, been around since 2007. They rate claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter." He'd turned the screen toward her. The ad's tax claim sat there with a little gauge on it, a whole range from True all the way down to Pants on Fire, which meant the claim had failed so completely that the meter had gone silly. The stadium claim, it turned out, was only mostly wrong, which earned it something in the middle.

The next morning Gabrielle boarded the bus holding a printout. "The ad took a number from one county and applied it to ours," she said. "The Truth-O-Meter called that Half True."

Marcus studied the paper. "My cousin's going to say the fact-checkers are biased."

"He can," Gabrielle said. "That's an opinion."

Priya leaned over the seat, pen already out. "So what's the actual number?"

"Ten dollars a year. Per family."

Priya crossed out eleven entries and sighed. "The people," she said, "are going to be so disappointed."

Marcus folded the printout and put it in his pocket. "I'm going to need this at lunch."

Oliver's mother had dropped him at Sunrise Travel for the afternoon because the dentist was next door, and because Mr. Adeyemi, the agent, had known him since he was five. The office smelled of old paper and coffee. On the back wall hung a giant world map with faint lines drawn across it, sideways and up and down, like graph paper wrapped around the world.

"You can find any city on Earth if you can read those lines," Mr. Adeyemi said, resting his coffee cup on the counter. "Latitude lines run sideways. Longitude lines run up and down. A city sits where one of each crosses. Nobody memorizes all the cities. You just read the numbers." He tapped a spot in Africa. "Cairo, about 30 degrees north latitude, 31 degrees east longitude." Oliver leaned close and traced the numbers with one finger, the way he had once traced the letters on his grandfather's frail old globe before it cracked in the move and had to be thrown out. He still felt bad about packing it badly. His grandfather had only said, "Maps outlive globes anyway," and Oliver had never been sure whether that was forgiveness or not.

A woman hurried in with a folder of papers, a customer named Mrs. Okafor who wanted to visit her sister in a city Oliver had never heard of. "Sister keeps saying, come before the heat, come before the heat," she told Mr. Adeyemi, "but she can never tell me why the heat comes when it comes." Mr. Adeyemi began flipping through a fat index of cities, muttering that his filing system was a disgrace and that if he could just win the office pool for most trips booked this month, he would finally buy a proper computerized system and retire the shoebox of index cards under his desk.

Oliver, meanwhile, was not looking up cities. He was looking at the tan patches. The Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the Kalahari, the Australian outback, the stretch across Mexico. He had noticed something at home on his wall map, and now, on this bigger one, he counted again, using the latitude lines like a measuring stick. The big hot deserts were not scattered anywhere. They lined up in two belts, one above the equator and one below, and when he read the numbers, the belts sat near 30 degrees north and near 30 degrees south. He checked one desert after another, and they kept landing on those numbers, as if the map had a rule it was following.

"Where sinking air warms up and dries out," Oliver said slowly, reading aloud from the small print under the map's legend. "That's why the deserts sit there, near 30 degrees north or south of the equator. It's a pattern."

"Find me the pattern for a rainforest, then," Mrs. Okafor said, half joking. Oliver ran his finger along the equator itself, where the green blobbiest jungles lived, past a poster of toucans dipping into flowers for nectar, past a caption about orchids that seemed able to colonize every wet branch in sight.

"Hot and wet at the equator, hot and dry at thirty," Oliver said. "So tell your sister the heat comes because her city sits in the dry belt. Thirty-two degrees north." Mrs. Okafor laughed and booked the ticket. Mr. Adeyemi slid the index card into his shoebox and said, "Two more bookings and that computer is mine."

Oliver went back to the map and put his finger on the empty blue Pacific, right at 30 degrees south, and waited to see if the rule would hold even there.

Nathaniel was eating cereal at the kitchen table with his laptop open when the group chat lit up. It was the Robotics Club chat, the one with eleven people in it, and someone named Marcus had just posted a screenshot. Nathaniel leaned closer, crumbs falling onto the keyboard. The screenshot showed a private chat between him and his friend Dev, and in it Nathaniel had written, "Honestly, Priya's robot arm design is garbage and she never listens to anyone." He had sent that two days ago, to one person, in a chat that said Just Dev and Nathaniel at the top.

His stomach dropped like an elevator with cut cables. Below the screenshot, Priya had typed a single line: "Cool. Thanks for that." Three people had reacted with the shocked face emoji. The room smelled suddenly too much like cinnamon cereal, and the fan above the stove hummed like nothing was wrong with the world.

Nathaniel closed his laptop, then opened it again. His first thought was that hackers had gotten in, which made him feel better for about four seconds. But nobody hacks a chat to steal a complaint about a robot arm. He had sent that message to exactly one person. If it was now in a different group chat, then Dev had shared it, because a private message only stays private if the person who receives it keeps it that way. Anyone with the message could screenshot it and pass it along. So the hidden cause wasn't hackers or a glitch. It was Dev.

He decided to test the idea before accusing anyone. He typed a new private message to Dev: "Hey, did you leave your phone unlocked at school today?" If Dev had no idea what he meant, the answer would sound confused. Instead Dev wrote back in eleven seconds: "Ok yeah. Marcus grabbed my phone in the cafeteria and went through my chats. I should've told you. I'm sorry." There it was, like finding the source of a leak in a pipe. Marcus, whose brother drove a delivery truck full of cargo from the airport and who never stopped talking about it, had hijacked Dev's phone and shipped Nathaniel's private words to the group like freight.

Nathaniel took a breath that tasted like cinnamon. First he sent Priya a message, not private this time, right in the group where everyone could see it: "That was a rude thing I wrote and I'm sorry. Your arm design has the best grip strength in the club." Then he wrote to Dev: "Next time change your password, and I'll try writing complaints in a journal made of actual paper."

He hit send, and the little checkmark appeared next to his apology, sitting there in public where everybody could watch Priya's reply load: "Meet me at the workbench tomorrow. Bring your grip strength ideas."

Mathis crouched between the rows of onions with his sketchbook balanced on his knee, and so far the page held exactly one thing: a sun with rays radiating out of it in every direction. His assignment was due Monday. Draw a food chain, his teacher had said, from the sun all the way to a top predator, and explain what happens if one link disappears. The garden was supposed to give him the whole chain for free, but so far it was giving him nothing but dirt under his nails.

"You're staring at an onion," said Priya, dropping down beside him with a bucket of water she was supposed to be carrying somewhere.

"I'm looking for aphids." Tiny green aphids meant the food chain's middle links. Aphids sucked juice from the onions, ladybugs ate the aphids, and the ladybug was his top predator. If he could find the bugs and sketch them, the poster would practically draw itself. He had already tried three plants in vain. Then he spotted them, a whole crowd of green specks clustered on an onion leaf, and right beside them, one round orange ladybug, steady as a stone. He copied the scene fast, before anything hopped away.

Priya leaned over his shoulder. "You made the leaf way too plain. Mrs. Okafor will want the cells. She's got that microscope in the shed, the one the bank donated when the garden almost got sold to pay somebody's mortgage." Mathis had forgotten about the microscope. He picked a thin sliver of onion skin, carried it to the shed, and slid it under the lens. The cells appeared like neat brick walls, each one boxed in. He labeled the cell wall, then the nucleus, easy. Then he reached the label that said cell membrane, and his pencil stopped. There was no line inside the boxes. Nothing. He turned the focus wheel back and forth until his eyes ached. "Maybe onion cells don't even have one," he muttered.

He tried a second slide, then a third. Same thing. The box stayed clean and single-lined, and the missing membrane stayed missing, no matter how he squinted. Then, staring until the brick shapes blurred, he understood. The membrane wasn't gone. It was pressed right up against the inside of the wall, so tight against it that it didn't show as its own line at all. The cell was full, that was all, so full that the membrane had nowhere to be except flat against the wall. He wrote "cell membrane" with an arrow pointing at the very edge of the box, right against the wall line, and drew a small tight second line beside it on his poster version so nobody else would hunt for it the way he had.

On the walk home he thought about the aphids, fat and crowded on that leaf, and the lone ladybug holding the border. Back at the garden, Priya was still watering. "Finished?" she called.

"Almost." He flipped his sketchbook open to the sun. "Watch this." He drew a big X through the ladybug, then over the aphids he wrote, in careful block letters, "100 of them by Friday."

The waiting room of Bright Smiles Dental smelled like mint and rubber gloves, and Landon had already read the poster about molars twice. His problem was bigger than a cavity. Next week he had to give a science report on how bees pollinate flowers, standing in front of the whole class, and ever since Ms. Rivera announced it, his hands got clammy and his brain went fuzzy. His mom said everyone gets nervous, which did not help at all.

In the corner, a girl about his age sat tracing something on the armrest of her chair. Up, across, down, across. Slow and steady, like she was drawing a square over and over. Landon watched her do it four times before his curiosity won.

"Are you drawing a map?" he asked.

She looked up like she'd been caught. "It's box breathing. My sister taught me before her recitals." She traced one side with her finger. "You breathe in for four, hold for four, breathe out for four, then hold for four. Then you do the whole pattern again." She demonstrated, sliding her finger up the invisible left wall while she inhaled, across the top while she held it, down the side while she breathed out, and along the bottom during the last hold.

Landon tried it right there, drawing his own square on the magazine cover in front of him. In four, hold four, out four, hold four. By the time the receptionist called his name, something surprising had happened: the fizzy feeling in his chest had shrunk to almost nothing.

In the chair, Dr. Okafor tilted her light and peered at his back teeth. "You're growing fast, Landon. Growing bodies sweat more, which is why showering every day and using deodorant becomes a significant part of the routine around your age. It's not a punishment, just biology." Landon grinned around the suction tube. Growth, sweat, breathing squares: it was a lot of new information, but he felt ready. Monday morning, standing in front of his class, he traced a square on the podium, one side for each count of four, and began: "Bees don't just visit flowers. They pollinate them."

Hazel had one shot left at the science demonstration contest, and her entry was falling apart in her hands. Her plan was to show the whole class something nobody could argue with: a physical change, which could go backward, and a chemical change, which could not. She had an ice cube in a dish, already half melted on the radiator, and a charred stick of wood she had burned at her uncle's campfire over the weekend. The ice would refreeze in the cafeteria freezer by fifth period. The stick was the problem. Somehow she had to prove, in front of everyone, that it could never be wood again.

Her friend Marcus wanted the opposite of proving things. He wanted to dismantle last year's winning project, a clunky volcano, and salvage its parts for his own robot arm, which was currently spreading through the science room like a virus. "Take the pump," he begged, unscrewing the base. "You don't need it. You've got a dish of water and a dead stick."

"That's the whole point," Hazel said. "The stick isn't dead. It's changed." But when Marcus lifted the volcano's lid, they found something better than a pump: a sealed glass jar with a candle stub and a long match. Marcus shrugged. It was equivalent to garbage to him. To Hazel it was a dare. Her old stick told the class nothing. They would look at it and say, so what, it's burnt, big deal. But if they watched wood burn in a jar, right there, and she asked them the impossible question afterward, they would have to think.

Fifth period came. The ice cube came back from the freezer solid and whole, and the class murmured approval. Then Hazel lit the match, touched it to the wood in the jar, and let the flame climb until it guttered out. She held up the jar so the back row could see the gray ash inside, the fog of water vapour on the glass. "The wood combined with the oxygen in there," she said. "What's left is ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. Now, who can turn it back into wood?" Nobody raised a hand, not even Marcus. He stared at the jar, screwdriver still in his fist, and said quietly, "You can keep the volcano parts."

Grandma Ruth was arriving on Saturday morning, and Piper had exactly one day to finish the backyard welcome plan: paper lanterns on the fence, lemonade, and the wobbly stepping stones she and Dad had laid last summer. But on Friday afternoon, Dad carried the loose braided rug out of the guest room, rolled it under his arm, and headed for the garage.

"Why are you taking Grandma's rug?" Piper asked, following him. She liked that rug. It was blue and gold, and it smelled faintly of cinnamon.

"Falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older," Dad said, setting the rug on a shelf. "In the whole United States. Mom told me that years ago, and I've never forgotten it."

Piper stood in the doorway, thinking. Grandma Ruth was sixty-eight. She hiked, and she could still do a cartwheel, though she claimed her knees filed complaints afterward. Still, the number Dad had said hung in Piper's mind like a question. She looked down the hallway: the rug gone, the floor bare, the bathroom door right there. Then she remembered the backyard. The stepping stones. Wobbly ones.

She ran outside and tested them, one at a time, pressing each with her sneaker like a doctor pressing a knee. The third stone rocked sideways with a squeak of gravel. That one, and the one by the fence, would tip under a foot that wasn't watching. She tried an experiment: she walked the path while carrying a tray of lemonade glasses, the way she'd carry it tomorrow, and nearly lost her balance when the third stone lurched. That settled it.

"Grandma's going to walk this path," Piper told Dad at dinner. "To see the lanterns. If a fall is the leading cause of injury death for people sixty-five and older, then a tipping stone is like a rug that fights back." Dad put down his fork. After dinner, the two of them knelt in the fading light with a bag of paver sand, tucking it under each stone, patting it firm, testing, adding more. The dirt smelled cool and mineral, and the sand gritted under Piper's knuckles.

Saturday arrived warm and buoyant, the paper lanterns bobbing on their strings as though they wanted to float away. Grandma Ruth came through the gate, hugged Piper long and hard, and then paused on the path. "These feel solid," she said, stepping carefully, heel to toe, heel to toe. "Someone nurtured this walkway."

"That was me," Piper said, holding out the lemonade. "And there's more. I have a whole list of things I'm checking before you go anywhere. The garage steps are next."

Grandma Ruth laughed and took her hand. "Then lead on, inspector. But first, show me how to make those lanterns."

Ariana sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page titled "Mi familia." Her Spanish homework was to write five full sentences about her family and pets, and so far she had two: "Mi mamá es alta" and "Tengo un gato negro." The rest of the page glared back at her, blank. Her cat, Biscuit, walked across the notebook as if to volunteer, and she lifted him off and set him on the floor. "You can't be every sentence," she told him.

The problem was her grandmother, Abuela Rosa, who lived two floors down in the same building. Abuela had sent a letter, an actual paper letter, and Mom had put it on the fridge. In it, Abuela wrote about a new restaurant in her old neighborhood where the food was wonderful but the service was strange. We waited forty minutes at the end, she wrote, sitting with empty plates, and no one ever brought us the bill. Finally another customer said something to the waiter and the bill came right away. I don't know what she said. Ariana read the letter three times. How could a bill arrive only after certain words were spoken? There had to be a hidden rule, some sentence waiters were listening for. She wondered if it was like a secret knock, and if she could find out what it was.

Ariana was skeptical at first that a phrase could matter that much. She tested her idea by calling her cousin Mateo, whose Spanish was better than hers. "If you wanted the waiter to bring the check," she asked, "what would you say?" Mateo answered without hesitating. "La cuenta, por favor." He said it meant "The bill, please." Ariana wrote it down, then said it out loud four times until it felt smooth. So the waiter hadn't been ignoring anyone. Nobody had asked. The words were the whole cause, invisible until you knew them.

She wrote back to Abuela in a letter of her own, which pleased her because Abuela loved mail. At the top, Ariana copied her homework sentences too: "Tengo una abuela que come en restaurantes. Mi abuela es divertida. Tengo un gato negro y juguetón." Then she added, "At the restaurant, you can say 'La cuenta, por favor.' It means 'The bill, please.'" She sealed the envelope and carried it downstairs herself, Biscuit trotting behind her like a small black shadow.

A week later a reply arrived. I used your words at the restaurant, Abuela wrote, and the bill came in two minutes. I thought I was too old to learn from an eleven-year-old, but I changed my mind. Ariana read that line twice, feeling something warm spread through her, and she had already decided her next letter would teach Abuela how to describe Biscuit. "Mi gato es negro," she practiced to the ceiling, "y mi abuela es la mejor."

Cameron wanted his street to look like it was actually sinking into the paper, the way the avenues in his favorite graphic novels did, buildings leaning toward each other until they vanished somewhere far below the edge. Ms. Ro had shown the class one-point perspective on Monday: a dot on the horizon, then ruler lines running toward it like ropes. Cameron had forgotten the ruler today, so he had to devise a substitute, and he scavenged through the studio's crowded supply shelf until he found a long wooden stirring stick, straight enough to trust.

He drew the vanishing point first, a small dot that he pretended was a doorway to another version of the street. Every roofline and curb had to aim at that doorway. When he leaned close and sighted along the stick, he could almost see the buildings folding inward, tugging each other down the page like the whole street was sliding into the dot. He tested one idea to be sure the trick was real: he drew a line he guessed would hit the dot, then laid the stick on top, and found it missed by a thumb's width. So the eye was a liar. The ruler-stick was the truth. He erased and redrew.

Across the table, Priya, age nine, was painting a portrait of her cat. She had made the cat's nose an unfortunate shade of green yesterday, let it dry overnight, and today she brushed clean water over it to soften the edges. The green moved. It smeared sideways in a slow tide across the cat's cheek, and Priya gasped like the cat itself had twitched.

"It dried," she said. "Dried things aren't supposed to run. Dried glue doesn't run."

Cameron came over and touched the edge of the smear with his fingertip. It came away faintly green. "Ms. Ro said watercolour paint is pigment bound with gum arabic," he said. "That's why it can dissolve again in water even after it's dried." He watched Priya's face do the same thing his had done when the stick proved his guessed line wrong, that flicker of a hidden rule suddenly becoming visible.

"So it's like it's only pretending to be permanent," Priya said. "A hypothetical cat that stays put until water shows up."

"Exactly. Your cat is a spy who dissolves when the rain comes."

Priya turned the smear into a swirl of whiskers, and the accidental green became grass in a reflection, a cat looking into a puddle. Cameron went back to his street and drew the puddle's edge with lines running to the vanishing point, so that even the reflection obeyed the doorway. He held the stick up to check it one last time.

"Bullseye," he said, and drew the dot's tiny doorframe around it.

Ryan had measured himself against the coat hooks in the hallway every Sunday since September, and today he finally had proof. He stood in Exam Room 4 with his shoes off, staring at the pencil marks on the doorframe of his memory, while Dr. Patel clicked through something on her screen.

"Four inches in ten months," she said. "That's a sprint, even for twelve."

"My mom thinks I'm going to be seven feet tall," Ryan said. "I told her the doorways aren't proportional to that plan, and she said we'd move."

Dr. Patel laughed and turned the monitor toward him. "Want to see why you're growing so fast? This is your left hand from today's X-ray."

The image was ghostly and gray, and Ryan perceived faint dark lines running near the ends of each bone, like tiny gaps in a fence. He leaned closer. "Is that a fracture? Do I have eleven fractures?"

"Those are your growth plates," she said. "Bones grow longer at the growth plates near their ends."

Ryan squinted. "So the middle of the bone just sits there doing nothing, and the ends do all the work?"

"Basically, yes."

He thought about that. The doorframe marks hadn't been even, either. Half an inch one month, an inch the next, then nothing for weeks, then a jump. It was like the erosion on the creek bank behind his school, slow and invisible until suddenly the shape had changed. Then a question landed in his stomach like a dropped marble. "Wait. Do the plates ever stop?"

"Once they close after puberty, a person stops getting taller," Dr. Patel said. "Closed means sealed. Done."

"So there's a deadline." Ryan sat up straighter. "Can you tell from the X-ray how close mine are?"

She tapped the screen. "See how wide and dark those lines are? Wide and open means lots of runway left. Narrow and pale means the countdown's nearly over."

That was all Ryan needed. He asked for the facts, memorized them, and spent the next week running an experiment. He borrowed his friend Desmond's little sister's growth chart app, and he tested a hypothesis: if his dad had stopped growing at fourteen, and his uncle at seventeen, then the family plates closed late, and Ryan had time. He tracked his uncles' heights at Thanksgiving like a detective, and Grandma pulled out a box of old report cards with heights penciled on the back. The data was beautiful. Late closers, all of them.

At his checkup the next June, Ryan had grown another two inches, and Dr. Patel held up the new X-ray next to the old one. The lines were still wide and dark.

"Runway," Ryan said, grinning.
