"Runway," she agreed, and printed him a copy to take home. On the way out, he taped it to the refrigerator at exactly his own eye level, which, he suspected, would not be his eye level for long.

Mila leaned her bicycle against the railing outside the bank and noticed the front tyre was flat, soft all the way around, with a hiss she could not hear but could imagine. She had ridden there to deposit a birthday cheque from her grandmother, and now the deposit would have to wait, because riding home on a flat would wreck the rim. In her backpack she had a repair kit her uncle had sent with a note, and she had never once used it.

She sat on the wide stone step beside the doors and unfolded the note. "Tyre levers go under the bead, three of them spaced around, then spoon the tyre off," her uncle had written in his careful, diligent handwriting. "Find the puncture, patch it, pump it up. You can interpret a flat two ways: bad luck, or a chance to learn something. Your choice." Mila read it twice, then dug out the levers, three curved plastic strips, and the little hand pump.

A security guard came out on his break and watched her work the first lever under the edge of the tyre. "You want to hook that second one a few inches along," he said, "and clip the third to a spoke." She did it, and when all three were set, the tyre popped loose and she could pull the tube out. As she ran her fingers along the rubber to find the hole, a spoke nicked her knuckle and a bead of blood rose up. She stuck it in her mouth.

"Put a plaster on that and let the air at it," the guard said. "Dries out faster that way."

A woman waiting by the doors shook her head. "My nurse said the opposite. A thin layer of petroleum jelly keeps the surface moist, and that helps it heal and can reduce scarring." The two of them went back and forth while Mila held the tube under the fountain by the wall, watching for bubbles. One small stream rose from a spot the size of a pinhead, near the valve. She marked it with the crayon from the kit, roughed it up with the sandpaper, spread the glue, and pressed the patch on until her thumb ached.

Then she took the small jar from the kit's zip pocket, dabbed petroleum jelly on her knuckle, and covered it with a plaster from her pencil case. "I'm going with the moist version," she said, holding up her finger. She tucked the tube back inside the tyre, seated the bead with her thumbs, and pumped until the tyre was firm enough to bounce a little when she pressed it. Inside the bank, she slid the cheque and the deposit slip through the slot at the counter. On the way out she rang the bell on her handlebars once, for the guard, and pedalled home over the bridge with the front tyre humming on the pavement.

Grayson had one week to turn a primary source into an actual answer, and his grandfather's attic had exactly one box labeled OLD PAPERS. The assignment wanted him to use something written at the time, not a textbook, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had guessed the answer would be gold, because everyone in his class would guess gold, and he wanted something better than the obvious.

Grandpa set the box on the kitchen table beside a rolled-up wall map he'd taken down from the hall. "That map's from my teaching days," he said. "You can spread it out when you need a break." Inside the box, under church programs and a ribbon from a prestigious agricultural fair, Grayson found a small leather book. The handwriting was cramped, and the ink had bled through the thin pages in places, so some words dissolved into pale blue shadows he could only guess at.

The diary belonged to a great-great-something named Elias Ward, and the first entry was dated April 1852. Grayson read slowly, hunting for the word gold. It never came. Instead Elias wrote about a letter from his brother in Iowa, describing soil so dark it "stains the boots," and about a failed mill back east, and about land selling for a dollar and a quarter an acre. Grayson sat back. His easy answer had just collapsed. He decided to test a new one: maybe people moved for cheap land and work, and the gold story was only part of it. He counted the reasons Elias gave across four entries, and land came up in every single one.

When his cousin Marisol arrived to borrow the map for her own homework, the two of them unrolled it on the living room floor. It showed the Roman Empire, not America at all. "You have to trace the biggest border," Marisol said, "for my teacher." Grandpa leaned in the doorway. "Biggest it ever got was around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan," he said. "Britain in the northwest, all the way to Mesopotamia in the east." Grayson and Marisol ran their fingers along the edge together, from the top corner of Britain across to the far eastern edge, and it took a long time, longer than either of them expected.

Marisol asked whether the empire lasted like that. "No, it got smaller after," Grandpa said, and rolled the map shut, and that single word, smaller, made something click for Grayson. Elias had written that his town back east was shrinking too, mills closing, neighbors leaving. Growing big and then shrinking had a consequence: people went looking for somewhere else. He copied three lines from the diary into his notebook, word for word.

Then he noticed the signature inside the back cover. Not Elias Ward. Ellen Ward, 1852. He flipped to the front again and read the April entry more carefully. "My husband reads this to me and I hold the pen," Ellen had written in the first line, which Grayson had skimmed right past. The settler's diary he needed had been written by the settler's wife, all along. "Grandpa," he called toward the kitchen, "did anyone in the family ever know Ellen wrote this?" Grandpa came back drying his hands on a towel and bent over the page for a long moment. "Well," he said, "they do now."

Ellie swung her bike into the gas station parking lot just as Marcus pedaled in behind her, both of them breathing hard. The afternoon heat shimmered off the pavement, and the drink cooler inside was calling their names. They had exactly three dollars each, saved from dog-walking money they cherished all week for this moment: the giant fountain sodas at Gas-N-Go, the biggest cups in town.

"Race you to the cooler!" Marcus shouted.

They burst through the door and stopped dead. A hand-written sign hung on the cooler: LARGE CUPS, 50 CENTS. Under it, another sign: ICE, SOLD OUT. Beside the register, a small table of last-year's water bottles read $1.75, while a full rack of them by the door read 99 cents.

"Wait, why are those two dollars and those under a dollar?" Marcus asked, pointing. "Same water."

Ellie frowned. The shelves near the register were nearly bare, with only six bottles left. The rack by the door was stacked to the top, so full nobody could reach the back rows. She picked up the 99-cent bottle and turned it over like a detective examining evidence. "Nobody's buying these because they're way over there," she said slowly. "And everybody grabs these because they're right here where you pay. So the close ones cost more because more people want them, and there aren't many left."

"So the store decides the price?" Marcus said.

"No way," Ellie said. "It's us. We decide it by what we'll pay. If we all refused to buy the close ones, they'd have to make them cheaper."

They argued about it all the way to the counter, where the clerk, a teenager named Dana, was taping a fresh price sign over the old one on the fountain machine. "Careful," Dana said. "Large sodas just went up to a dollar. We're almost out of large cups." Behind her, Ellie saw a single sleeve of large cups left, and a line of sweaty customers forming at the door.

"A dollar!" Marcus groaned. "Yesterday it was fifty cents!"

Ellie's mind spun. Then Dana pointed at a mountain of small cups by the syrup machine, hundreds of them, untouched. "Small ones are still fifty cents," Dana said. "We've got a million of those."

Ellie grabbed two small cups. "It's like scissors," she announced, paying Dana. "My grandpa told me about this guy named Alfred Marshall, who wrote a book in 1890 called 'Principles of Economics.' He compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"Both what?" Marcus asked, filling his cup from the root beer nozzle.

"Buyers and sellers," Ellie said. "You were right that buyers set the price, and I was right that sellers do. We're both right, like the two blades. Neither one alone can cut anything." She held up her cup triumphantly. "And today, both blades say: buy small, because small is plentiful and cheap."

They carried their sodas outside to the concrete curb, where the air conditioner's thermostat hummed against the wall, keeping the store cool. Marcus took a long sip and grinned. "Best fifty cents I ever spent."

Ellie clinked her styrofoam cup against his like a toast. "To Alfred Marshall," she said, "and his scissors."

Every August, watering Grandma's tomato beds was a ritual: fill the can at the spigot, haul it down the gravel path, pour, trudge back. Jade had assumed the tomatoes needed her, but by the third trip her arms burned, and she began to think the tomatoes mostly needed somebody with stronger shoulders.

Grandma was at the picnic table with her coffee, reading, while Jade lugged the can again. "My arms are going to fall off," Jade said.

"Farmers along the Nile had the same problem," Grandma said. "They used a shaduf." She pointed her cup at the tool shed. "Your grandfather built one for the pond years ago. It's behind the rakes." That was all she said, and she went back to her book.

Jade found it leaning against the wall: a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy stone wired to the other, balanced on a post. She hauled it to the pond, dipped the bucket, and pulled down on the rope. The stone rose, the bucket swung up over the bank, and the water poured out toward the beds. It still took work, but it took half the work, and Jade stood there dripping and grinning, moving bucket after bucket. It was so simple it felt unfair. One heavy thing lifting another, so nobody's arms had to do it all.

Then she remembered Monday. Her history teacher had asked the class to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and Jade's rough draft was one flat sentence: the treaty punished Germany after World War I. Mrs. Okafor had written, "But how? Show me." Jade sat down on the gravel, still holding the shaduf rope, and thought about punishment. Germany had been made to carry payments so heavy they never seemed to end, like being handed a watering can that never got lighter. People who feel crushed year after year look for someone to lift the weight, and someone had promised he could. She couldn't see a country or an armistice the way she could see this pole, but the shape was the same, a burden doing something over time. She pulled out her notebook and wrote: imagine carrying the can forever, and imagine the person who says, put it down.

"Did you figure out your homework out here?" Grandma asked, coming down the path with the empty coffee cup.

"I think the treaty is a watering can," Jade said, and hauled up another bucket.

The floorboards in Grandma Ruth's attic creaked as Levi and his cousin Marisol set up two folding chairs. In two hours, the whole family would gather downstairs for Grandpa Joe's seventieth birthday party, and the two of them had promised to perform a five-minute improv scene, even though Levi had never done improv in his life.

"Rule one," Marisol said, tapping the chair like a game show host. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you add something. So if I say, 'We're astronauts landing on a cheese moon,' you don't say, 'No, that's silly.' You say, 'Yes, and the smell is making me hungry.'"

"That sounds easy," Levi said.

It was not easy. Every time Marisol made an offer, Levi's brain revolved around all the things that could go wrong, and out of his mouth came a dodge. "Um, I guess so," he said to the cheese moon. "Uh, okay," he said when she suggested they were being chased by a vacuum cleaner. Marisol pulled a small notepad from her pocket and started making tally marks, one for every um and uh. After ten minutes she turned the page toward him: twenty-three marks.

Levi stared at the tallies like they were evidence at a trial. He had thought his problem was not knowing what to say, but the marks showed a different pattern. The ums appeared exactly when an offer arrived, right at the moment of choice. He decided to run a test. Instead of filling the gap with a sound, he would stay silent for a beat, then say the words "Yes, and" and let them carry him wherever they wanted.

They started the scene again. Marisol said, "Our spaceship runs on pickle juice." Levi paused, silent, letting the pause sit there. "Yes, and we're almost out, so we have to land at the space diner." Marisol's eyebrows shot up. She kept the scene going, and the tally marks slowed, then stopped. By the third run, she put the notepad away entirely and started laughing so hard she fell off her chair.

Downstairs, the smell of Grandpa Joe's lemon cake drifted up the attic stairs. Levi heard chairs scraping, the screen door banging, and Grandma Ruth calling that the show would start in five minutes. Marisol grabbed his arm. "One last treaty," she said. "Whatever happens down there, nobody says no, not even once." Levi shook her hand, and they headed for the stairs, where the first row of relatives, looking cheerful but slightly obstinate about being entertained, was already waiting. Marisol leaned over and whispered, "We're two penguins who opened a lemonade stand in Antarctica." Levi let the pause hang there, took a breath, and said, "Yes, and business is about to pick up."

Stella's pencil hovered over the paper, and the paper was winning. In art cabin three, everyone else had already drawn a street with one-point perspective: two rows of buildings whose edges ran uphill and downhill toward a single dot, the vanishing point, where the whole road disappeared. Hers looked like a street built by a drunk giant. The left side tilted one way, the right side the other, and the road climbed instead of receding.

She wanted this badly, because tomorrow the camp was holding a small gallery night, and the pottery instructor, an artisan from the town who sold glazed bowls at the market, had promised to trade one bowl for any drawing she liked. Stella had her eye on a blue-green one with a wobbly rim. She also wanted to beat Marcus, who kept leaning over and saying, "Mine looks like a photograph, Stella. Yours looks like a melted crayon."

She decided to test an idea instead of guessing. First she retraced the road with her ruler and saw the problem: her building lines weren't parallel with each other before they angled in, so they ran to two different vanishing points instead of one. Two vanishing points meant two roads, and two roads meant melted crayon. She marked a single dot with a pushpin, tied a piece of string to it, and pulled the string tight to guide each line. The string made a faint sound, a small humming like a plucked guitar, and she pretended it was the street singing itself into place. Pin to corner, line. Pin to corner, line. Slowly a real street appeared, a candy shop, a lamppost, a mailbox, all obedient, all sliding toward the dot.

But her street was empty, so she added a boy juggling on the sidewalk and, near him, a ball resting on the pavement. The ball looked wrong. No matter how she shaded the rounded side of it, the ball seemed to hover a little above the ground, like it was floating an inch of air, refusing to land. She erased the shadow, drew it again, shaded the whole shadow evenly. Still hovering. Marcus leaned over. "Nice balloon," he said.

Stella glared at the drawing, then at the actual sunny porch step outside, where a soccer ball sat in the sun. She went out and knelt beside it. The shadow on the step wasn't the same darkness all the way across; the outer edge looked soft and gray, but the part right under the ball, in the narrow space where the ball touched the step, went almost black, the darkest shadow of all. She hadn't shaded that spot at all. Back inside, she pressed her pencil down hard in the tiny area where the ball met the pavement, making it the darkest mark on the whole street, and left the rest of the shadow lighter. The ball dropped onto the ground like it had been waiting for permission.

At gallery night the artisan stood in front of her drawing for a long moment. She tapped the place where the ball touched the street and said, "You saw it. Most people never look at the dark part where the ball touches the ground." Stella retrieved the blue-green bowl from the trade table with both hands, and Marcus, standing behind her with his photograph-perfect street, said, "Okay. Fine. That one's better."

Naomi spread her graph paper across the kitchen table and wrote "SIMPLE" at the top of one column and "COMPOUND" at the top of the other. She was saving her birthday money, forty dollars a year, and her mother had said, "Five years. Figure out which account pays more." The simple account added three dollars for every hundred, every year, straight across. The compound one added three dollars on whatever was already there, including the interest from before. She worked the simple column fast. The compound column made her stop and squint, because the numbers climbed a tiny bit faster each year, like something growing quietly underground.

Her cousins burst in before she finished. Marcus waved a crumpled certificate. "Toytown stock. Uncle Rick gave it to me last summer." Priya held up a fancy printed sheet. "I got a Toytown bond. Same company." Toytown had gone bankrupt in the spring, and every kid on the block had heard about it.

"Mine's a stock," Marcus said. "Stocks sound bigger."

"I don't even know what a bond is," Priya admitted.

Naomi tapped her pencil. The word bankruptcy had shown up in her mother's newspaper pile, and one afternoon she had read enough of an article to provoke a question she'd been chewing on ever since: when a company died, who got paid first? She had made an inference from the article's grumbling quotes, and now she wanted to test it. "Trade me," she said suddenly. "Straight across. My next two weeks of allowance for your bond."

Priya stared. Marcus laughed so hard he knocked over the lemonade. "You'd trade real money for paper from a dead company?"

"Twenty minutes," Naomi said. "Then decide." She flipped her graph paper over and wrote fast, then handed Priya a note:

"Priya. If we're right about the order they pay people, your sheet is ahead of his in line. Stocks are last in line, and often get nothing at all. I'll still buy it from you either way, but only for a dollar. That way you can't lose much. Your choice. Naomi."

While Priya read, Marcus kept gloating, which provoked nothing but Naomi's patience. Priya looked up. "Last in line? So Marcus's stock is behind mine?"

"Only if my inference is right," Naomi said. "Grandma's neighbor worked at a bank. Let's ask her, but I'm asking, and nobody talks but me."

Mrs. Okafor, three doors down, was watering her tomatoes. She listened, wiped her hands, and said, "When a company goes bankrupt, bondholders get paid back before stockholders. Stockholders are last in line, and often they get nothing."

The walk home was quiet except for Marcus's sneakers. He stopped at the driveway. "Okay. I changed my mind. Your compound interest thing, the one you were drawing? Teach it to me and I'll trade you my stock for Priya's bond. She said yes already." He pointed at Priya, who was grinning and holding out the crumpled certificate.

"Deal," Naomi said, and she cleared a space at the table between her two columns. "Now watch what happens in year three."

Marcus pulled up a chair.

The deodorant aisle smelled like a fake pine forest, and Ethan stood in front of it holding two dollars and thirty-seven cents in his palm. His mother had sent him in for cough syrup while she circled the parking lot, but on the way to the register he had spotted the gel deodorant with the lightning bolt on it, the same kind Marcus used, and before he really thought about anything he had it under his arm. Now he was doing the math. The cough syrup cost exactly two dollars and thirty-seven cents, and he had exactly that. The deodorant cost four dollars and fifty cents.

"It's a paradox," his sister Lily would have said if she were there, "wanting to be the kind of kid who buys deodorant and also the kind who brings home the medicine." She wasn't there, but he could hear her anyway, which was annoying. He envied Marcus, who seemed to have everything figured out, deep voice and gym bag and all. Ethan's own voice still cracked in the middle of class like a bad radio.

At the register, the pharmacist, a woman named Dara with reading glasses on a chain, rang up both items before he could decide. "That's six eighty-seven," she said. His face went hot. He mumbled that he only had the two thirty-seven, and that the deodorant had been, sort of, an accident.

While Dara took the deodorant back, his phone buzzed. It was a text from Lily, and attached was a page she had been reading for her health class: a diagram of a brain with a shaded area near the front. The caption said the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. Ethan read it twice. So the part of him that was supposed to plan ahead and stop himself from grabbing things was still, literally, under construction. That was almost a relief.

"So that's the prefrontal cortex," he said out loud, pointing at the shaded spot, "and mine's still loading." Dara leaned over the counter to look and laughed. "Mine took until about twenty-five, if it's any comfort." She slid the cough syrup across to him and kept the gel deodorant in a small pile behind the register, marked with a sticky note that said HOLD FOR ETHAN.

"For next week," she said. "When you've saved up. Planning ahead, right?" Ethan nodded, put his phone away, and walked out to the car with the change still warm in his hand and a plan already forming for the four dollars and fifty cents he was going to earn mowing Mrs. Okafor's lawn on Saturday.

The sign in aisle six stopped Aaron cold. Storm Cocoa Puffs, the cereal he'd been saving for, had jumped from four dollars to six fifty. The shelf behind the sign was nearly empty, just three battered boxes left. His mom had given him exactly five dollars and told him to pick a box while she grabbed Grandma's prescription at the pharmacy counter.

He picked up a box anyway and turned it over, as if the answer might be printed under the ingredients, next to the part about polymer packaging that kept it fresh. Three boxes left. Everyone in town must want this cereal because of the storm that had knocked out power for two days and kept delivery trucks off the roads. When lots of people want something that's running out, he figured, the store can charge more, and they do.

An older man in a gray coat reached past Aaron for the last box on the top shelf, then paused. "You were here first, son." He held it out. Aaron looked at his five dollars and shook his head. "I can't afford it anymore. It went up." The man's face went vague for a second, then he set the box back. "Everything went up this week. My wife's heart pills went up twelve dollars."

"Are you going to stop buying them?" Aaron asked, then winced, because it sounded rude.

The man laughed, but not meanly. "Of course not. She needs them." He tapped the box on the shelf. "I'll skip this, though." He walked off toward the pharmacy with his small cart.

Aaron wandered that way too, because the cereal he could afford, the store brand, was stocked in the next aisle over, and it was on sale, two for five. Piles of it. Nobody was fighting over it. His theory was holding up: scarce plus wanted meant expensive, plentiful meant cheap. But the pills kept bugging him. Twelve dollars more, and the man didn't even hesitate. He'd compared it in his own head, buying the pills versus skipping cereal, and the pills won without a fight.

At the counter, Aaron found his mom and the pharmacist, Ms. Reyes, sliding a white paper bag across. "Same price as always for the generic," Ms. Reyes said. "The brand-name went up again, but almost everyone keeps buying it anyway." She noticed Aaron listening. "That's called inelastic," she said. "People buy it no matter what the price does."

"Inelastic," Aaron repeated, testing the word.

Ms. Reyes nodded and turned to the next customer.

On the way out, Aaron recounted his finds to his mom: the cereal, the sale, the man with the gray coat and the twelve dollars. She listened the whole way through the parking lot, then stopped by the cart return and held up the pharmacy bag. "So what you're saying is, Grandma's medicine is like a need, and your cereal is like a want."

"Basically." Aaron hugged the two store-brand boxes to his chest. "And next week, when the trucks come, the price of mine drops. The pills won't."

His mom smiled and unlocked the car. "Get in, economist."

Charles had a system, and the system had a flaw. The flaw was the letter F.

For three days he had studied the eye chart the school nurse had photocopied and sent home. He could recite it frontwards: E, F, P, T, O, Z, all the way down to the tiny row that looked like ants carrying crumbs. The chart was older than anyone could remember, the nurse said, a dusty poster that had been in the clinic since forever, and Charles planned to recite it perfectly at Saturday's eye appointment so nobody would know his left eye had gone fuzzy. If he passed, he could keep playing goalie without his cousin Marcus announcing, to the entire neighborhood, that Charles couldn't see a soccer ball until it hit him.

His little sister Dee wandered into the kitchen, where the photocopy was taped to the refrigerator. "That's mine now," she said. "I'm starting an eye hospital in the garage. I already have a tongue depressor and half a stethoscope."

"You can't have a hospital with one patient."

"I'll circulate flyers," Dee said. "Everyone on this street has eyes. That's my market."

Saturday morning, the optometrist's office smelled like plastic and peppermint. Charles was ready. The doctor, a small woman with purple glasses, sat him in a chair and pointed at a wall chart.

"Read the top line."

"E," Charles said confidently. Then "F, P, T, O, Z," sailing down the rows without a single mistake, like a boy with vision sharp enough to count a mosquito's eyebrows.

The doctor looked at him. Then she walked to the wall, pressed a button, and the chart rolled up with a snap. A different chart rolled down, one Charles had never seen.

"Read this one."

Charles opened his mouth. Nothing came out. The letters were strangers, blurry gray smudges, like an intestine photograph in his science textbook, all coiled and mysterious and definitely not something he could identify from across a room.

"That chart you memorized," the doctor said, "was Herman Snellen's chart, the rows of shrinking letters he developed in 1862." She smiled. "Kids try it every month. The Snellen chart is older than your great-grandparents. Some of them, older than your great-great-great-grandparents."

"You could have told me there were two charts," Charles said.

"Where's the fun in that?"

An hour later Charles stood blinking in the waiting room in his first pair of glasses, round silver ones, and the world snapped into focus like a TV with the antenna finally straightened. He could read the gum wrapper on the counter. He could read the exit sign. He could read Dee's flyer, which she had apparently made during his exam, circulating it to every seat: DEE'S EYE HOSPITAL, GRAND OPENING, MY BROTHER IS THE FIRST PATIENT.

"You're not touching my eyeballs," Charles said.

"It's unanimous between me and the tongue depressor," said Dee, and she took his hand and marched him toward the garage.

Ellie set the cutting board on the picnic table at the back of the yard, where the light was good and the smell of chopped vegetables wouldn't fill the kitchen. Tonight was her turn to make dinner, and she had promised her family potato soup with real onions, not the dried flakes from a jar. Her little brother Marcus sat on the grass nearby, sketching on a pad of paper. He wanted to depict the whole meal in a drawing, soup pot and all, so he could hang it on the fridge when the food was done.

She halved the first onion and began to chop. Within a minute her eyes stung and water ran down her cheeks. Marcus looked up from his drawing, alarmed, then his own eyes began to stream too, even though he was three steps away and hadn't touched the onion at all.

"You're crying," he said, wiping his face with his sleeve. "Why does a vegetable make people cry?"

"I'm not crying," Ellie said, sniffling. "I'm mad at this onion." But she kept thinking about it while she chopped. The tears had started only after she cut into it, not before, when the onion was whole on the table. Something had to be coming out of the onion when her knife went through it. She remembered her mother saying the cells inside a plant were like tiny sealed rooms. Cutting must break the cells open and release something, some kind of gas, and the gas had to be reaching their eyes. That would explain why Marcus was tearing up too, sitting nowhere near the cutting board. It would even explain why whole onions in the bag had never made anyone cry.

She decided to test the idea. She carried the board to the far corner of the yard, upwind of Marcus, so any gas drifting off would blow away from him instead of toward him. She made him stay by the picnic table with his drawing while she finished the chopping. From across the yard she called out, "Eyes still burning?"

"No," Marcus called back, surprised. He blinked hard and touched his eyelids. "They stopped. Hey, Ellie, is the gas why the soup in your picture looks like it's steaming? Because that's steam, not crying gas."

"That's steam, you gullible creature," she said, laughing through her own tears. She finished the last onion, dumped everything into the pot, and carried it inside, blinking the sting away.

After dinner, Marcus taped his drawing to the refrigerator, right beside the takeout menu from the tenants who rented the upstairs apartment. He tapped the little onion in the corner of the picture and said, "I'm going to draw tears on it, for science."

Edouard stood in Mrs. Okafor's kitchen holding a page of instructions she'd scribbled before hurrying out to her night shift. Bedtime at eight. Snack at seven. Emergency numbers on the fridge. He was thirteen and this was his first real babysitting job, and the two-dollar word for how he'd gotten it, according to his mother, was that he was "not impulsive like some boys," which he hoped was a compliment.

The child, Poppy, was three and wanted exactly one thing: to excavate the couch cushions until she found the lost button from her purple coat. She had been at it for twenty minutes, dragging cushions onto the floor like a little archaeologist, when Edouard noticed the kitchen had gone silent. Silent was wrong. He counted the sounds he should have heard: no humming, no cushion thumping, no small shoes on tile. He ran.

Poppy stood by the sink with a spray bottle in both hands, cap off, and a shiny wet smear across her chin. The label said all-purpose cleaner. Edouard's stomach dropped, but he crouched down and spoke slowly. "Did you drink some, or just touch it?" Poppy, proud of her honesty, said, "I licked it. Like a lollipop."

His phone was in the living room, and for one terrible second he couldn't remember any number except 911, which felt wrong for a lick. Then he remembered Mrs. Okafor tapping the fridge twice. Taped at eye level was a curled index card: Poison Help 1-800-222-1222. He called it, heart hammering, and a calm woman answered on the second ring. "This is poison control. What happened?" He told her: three-year-old, cleaner, a lick, a few minutes ago.

"Read me the label," she said. He did, squinting at the tiny print while Poppy tried to lick the bottle again and he held it above her head like a chandelier. The woman asked questions, then said a small lick of this one was usually nothing to worry about, but to give Poppy water and watch her for an hour, and to call back anytime, day or night. "Wait, it's almost nine at night," Edouard said. "You're still open?" "Any hour," she said. "Your call goes right to your local poison center."

He gave Poppy water in the good dinosaur cup and watched the clock like it owed him money. By eight thirty she was drowsy and complaining that her chin tasted "spicy," which the woman had said could happen. By nine she was asleep with the excavated button clutched in her fist, and Edouard texted Mrs. Okafor everything, ending with a question he genuinely wondered about: how many parents taped that card to the fridge, and how many never thought to?

When Mrs. Okafor came home at eleven, she read the texts twice, checked Poppy's sleeping face, and pressed twenty dollars into his hand instead of the agreed fifteen. "You called them before you panicked," she said. "That's the whole job." Edouard photographed the index card before he left, so he could make one for his own fridge, then stood on her porch in the cold, wondering whether the woman at poison control was still there, answering, somewhere in the dark.

Evelyn set her tray down at the end of the sixth-grade table, three seats away from Priya, who was picking at her pizza without looking up. Priya had skipped Evelyn's birthday sleepover on Saturday, and the text she sent had said only "can't come, sorry." No reason. No follow-up. On Sunday Evelyn had decided that Priya was selfish, full stop, and she had walked to school Monday radiating that decision like a heater.

She was also, in a diligent way, reading her older brother's psychology book at lunch, because she had a book report due Friday and no library pass. A page caught her eye. It described blaming someone's behavior on their character while ignoring the situation they were in. That was exactly what she'd done, she realized, except she hadn't ignored Priya's situation, because she didn't know it. Which was the problem. She didn't have the data.

"So what was the situation?" said Marcus, who had leaned over to steal her fries. "You don't know."

"I can find out," Evelyn said. She tore a corner from her brown bag, wrote a note, and folded it into a paper football. Then she flicked it across three seats. It hit Priya's milk carton. Priya unfolded it, read it, and looked over. Evelyn held up the psych book, then pointed at the empty chair beside her. A signal, she hoped, that said "truce, and also I have evidence."

Priya slid over with her tray. "What do you want."

"My brother's book says there's this thing," Evelyn said. "It's called the fundamental attribution error. A psychologist named Lee Ross named it in 1977." She showed Priya the page. "It's when you blame somebody's character instead of their situation. I did it to you. I called you selfish."

Priya stared at the page. "My grandmother had a stroke Friday night. We were at the hospital until Sunday. I didn't want to text the whole story, it felt weird." Her voice wobbled. "And I thought you'd be mad, so I didn't text at all, which was worse. Is she okay? She's okay, by the way. She yelled at a nurse about the jell-o, so she's fine."

"Then why weren't you answering me this morning?"

"I left my phone at the hospital," Priya said. "Mom's picking it up today. That's where I'm going after school, actually, if you want to come. Grandma keeps asking who ate all her grapes, and I need a witness that it wasn't me."

Evelyn closed the book. "I'll bring grapes."

Marcus reached across the table and took one of her fries anyway.

The bell hadn't rung yet, but Mr. Okafor's computer lab was already loud with keyboards. Nathan slid into his seat, logged in, and opened the group chat for the robotics club. The regional qualifier was in nine days, and nobody had agreed on who was bringing the backup battery pack. He typed his question, waited, and watched three other conversations scroll past without a single answer to his.

Across the row, Marcus hunched over his screen, tapping keys like he was squashing bugs. On the chat, a message from him shot to the top: WHERE ARE YOU. It sat there, thick and enormous. Below it, Priya replied within seconds: why are you yelling? i'm right here, chill.

Nathan blinked at the screen. Marcus hadn't been yelling. Nathan had heard him, and the loudest sound in the room was the heater rattling under the window, the same eccentric rattle it made every January. So why did Priya hear shouting? He looked again. Marcus's message was all capitals, every letter. Priya's was all lowercase. Nathan scrolled back through the last week of chat, and a pattern showed up fast: whenever somebody typed in capitals, the replies got defensive, jumpy, short. Whenever they typed normally, people answered calmly, even kindly.

He decided to test it. He typed a second question about the battery pack in regular letters and sent it, then leaned over. "Marcus, try asking again. Not all capitals. Just regular." Marcus gave him a suspicious squint, but he erased his draft and retyped it letter by letter, and Nathan watched him deliberately convert the giant blocky words into ordinary ones. where are you guys, we need to plan.

This time Priya answered in half a minute. here, sorry, was fixing my wheel. i can bring the battery pack if someone grabs the charger. Two more club members chimed in with offers, and within five minutes the whole supply list was sorted. Marcus stared at the screen like a magician had just pulled a rabbit out of it.

"So the caps were the problem," Marcus said slowly. "People read it like you're shouting at them."

"That's what it looked like from here," Nathan said. He felt a small twist of guilt anyway, remembering a message he'd sent his cousin last month in all capitals, and the cold one-line reply that had followed. He'd thought his cousin was just being moody.

Mr. Okafor called for attention and the screens went dark one by one. As they lined up, Marcus nudged Nathan's shoulder. "Next time something weird happens in the chat, you're investigating," he said. "Deal?"

The nurse's office smelled like disinfectus and old paper, and Grace sat on the crinkly paper of the cot while Mrs. Okafor fitted a pair of purple frames over her ears. The little hinge above each lens clicked as the temples folded out, and Grace felt the weight of them settle on her nose like a small, patient animal.

"I can see the poster," she said. The eye chart across the room, which had been a smear of gray all morning, now had letters on it, sharp as typed words. Even the crooked thumbtack in the corner of the sun safety poster was suddenly clear.

Mrs. Okafor smiled. "Dr. Patel said your prescription is mild. Nearsighted, which means the far stuff is blurry." She wrote something on a card. "Signs the paper for your mom, and you can go back to class."

Grace slipped out into the hallway, but instead of turning toward math, she stood still. The drinking fountain down the hall had a dent in it. The trophy case had fingerprints on the glass. All year she had thought the board was smudged and the posters were faded, and it had been her own eyes the whole time. That was the part that bugged her. Her little brother read at midnight with a flashlight and had perfect vision, and she had eaten her carrots and done everything right, or mostly right. She wanted to know the actual reason, and she wanted it before she got home and her mom asked why she needed glasses when Theo didn't.

At lunch she found Dr. Patel's pamphlet still folded in her jacket pocket, the one from the clinic visit last week. She read it at the picnic table outside, in the October sun. Under a heading about nearsightedness it said that studies show nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. Grace read the sentence twice. Then she did her own test, right there, because it was a thing she could check.

She made a list in her head. Theo played outside constantly, soccer and worms and whatever else. Priya, who sat in front of her and wore thick glasses, had told Grace once that she spent whole weekends gaming and rarely left the house. Grace herself had spent the last two summers indoors, drawing at her desk and postponing every walk because the air conditioning was better. She thought of three more kids with glasses and tried to remember whether she ever saw them at the park. She didn't. The kids who were always outside on weekends, like Marcus and his loud bike, were the ones squinting at nothing in class.

"So it wasn't the carrots," she said out loud, and Priya, across the table, laughed.

"Carrots can't fix weekends indoors," Priya said. "I'm negligent about daylight, according to my mom."

"I'm going outside this Saturday," Grace said. She lifted her new glasses and looked at the trees past the fence, each leaf separate for the first time. "First, I have to postpone my math homework. Somebody has to call my mom about these."

Kate had spent most of October guessing which kids were which by the shape of their hair, so when Coach Ruiz finally said "The scoreboard is right there, Alvarez, and you asked me if we won," she marched herself to the nurse's office before last period.

The nurse, Ms. Okafor, was trying to renovate a cardboard eye chart stand that a kindergartner had body-slammed during a fire drill. "Sit," she said, pointing with a roll of tape. "Letters getting blurry, or is everything a smudge?" Kate explained about the scoreboard, and about how the whiteboard looked like it had melted a little, especially the vertical lines. Ms. Okafor hummed and flipped lenses in a funny pair of frames, asking which looked better, one or two, one or two, until Kate's answers started sounding like a coin flip.

"Astigmatism," Ms. Okafor said at last. "Your eye bends light unevenly, so the lenses have to bend it unevenly too."

"Like a magic trick?"

"Like a very boring magic trick. The district's lens kit takes two weeks, but we have a loaner pair in your prescription." She dug through a drawer that appeared to contain one glove, three lollipops, and a small civilization of rubber bands, then produced a pair of purple glasses.

The world snapped into focus so hard Kate actually said "Oh" out loud. But then she tilted her head to scratch her ear, and the doorframe stretched, tall and skinny, like taffy. She froze, then straightened up slowly, watching the doorframe go back to normal. She turned her head again, and the bulletin board's squarish border leaned and widened like something out of a funhouse. She did it twice more, careful and slow, like a scientist and also like a dog chasing its own tail.

"Um, my glasses are haunted," she reported.

Ms. Okafor came over, and Kate demonstrated, tilting her head like a confused owl. "Ah," Ms. Okafor said. "Those are cylindrical lenses. They bend light more in one direction than in the other. Turn them sideways and everything stretches." Kate looked down at the lenses, turning them over in her hand, thinking that she was wearing tiny directional window washers on her face, and that this was the best school day she'd had in weeks.

"Can I keep them on for class?" she asked.

"Loaners are yours until your real pair comes in. Those will be permanent."

Kate slid them on and stopped in the doorway, staring at the hallway clock. "That's been there the whole year?"

"Since before you were born," said Ms. Okafor. On her way out, Kate noticed a teary first-grader waiting with an ice pack, and she handed him one of Ms. Okafor's drawer lollipops on her way past. "The nurse is really nice," she whispered. "And her glasses made my head look huge, so you'll feel great about your ice pack."

"Thanks," the boy said, squinting up at her. "Are you wearing a purple owl?"

"Close enough," said Kate.

The first thing Muhammad noticed about Camp Willowood was the canopy of oak branches over the swimming dock, so thick that the water looked green instead of blue. The second thing he noticed was Dana. She sat at the end of the dock every morning, gripping the edge, staring at the lane ropes like they might bite her.

"They're doing time trials Friday," his cabin mate Theo told him. "Dana's the fastest swimmer here, but she won't get in the water. She's been like that for weeks. Won't eat breakfast, won't sleep. Just sits."

Muhammad knew about not sleeping. Back in the spring, before his big math exam, he had lain awake for a whole month, his stomach in knots, until his grandfather taught him a trick. Breathe in for four counts, hold for four, out for six, and do it in bed at the same time every night. The breathing was boring, but boring was the point. It told his body the day was over. His stomach had finally settled, and the night before the exam, he had actually slept.

On Wednesday, Muhammad's own jitters arrived. Time trials meant the whole camp watching, and when he stood on the dock for practice, his heart hammered and his hands shook. He almost climbed back down. Then he remembered what his grandfather had said, and he tried the breathing right there, four in, four held, six out, three times. His hands went still. His focus got sharp, sharp enough that he swam his fastest lap of the summer.

He climbed out, dripping, and an idea formed. A nervous feeling right before you perform wasn't the enemy. His jitters had made him faster. But Dana hadn't felt nervous for one race. She'd felt awful for weeks, and that was different. He couldn't see inside her any more than he could see the roots under the oak trees, but the pattern was there, hiding in plain sight.

He walked to the end of the dock. "You're going to think I'm annoying," he said.

"Probably," Dana said, not looking up.

"Jitters before a race are normal. They can actually sharpen you. But feeling this bad for weeks isn't the same thing." He sat down beside her. "That kind doesn't go away on its own. You should talk to the camp nurse. Or your counselor. Somebody."

Dana finally looked at him. "I thought it would just go away."

"I did too, for a month," Muhammad said. "It didn't. Then I talked to my grandpa, and we fixed the sleeping part first."

She stared at the green water for a long moment. Then she stood up, brushed off her shorts, and walked toward the office building, her flip-flops slapping the boards.

Friday came, and the camp gathered under the oaks where the ivy seemed to flourish even in the shade. Muhammad stood on the blocks, heart hammering, hands steady. In lane four, Dana pulled her cap on and shook out her arms. When the whistle blew, she hit the water first.

Tyler kept the box on his lap the whole ride, because the bus was notorious for potholes, and the last thing he wanted was his first phone sliding under a seat. It was a hand-me-down from his grandfather, handed over at the kitchen table that morning while Grandpa ate toast. Grandpa had weighed it in his palm and laughed. "The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Two and a half pounds, like a bag and a half of sugar." He had set it down gently after that, as if it might bruise.

Now Tyler slid the phone out and it did seem impossibly light, lighter than his math binder, lighter than the sandwich in his backpack. He couldn't feel the difference between two and a half pounds and nothing much unless he had something to compare, so he borrowed Marcus's half-filled water bottle from the seat pocket and held it in one hand and the phone in the other. The bottle was heavier. He added Marcus's science book to the bottle hand and thought about Grandpa holding a brick against his ear the whole walk down a New York sidewalk. His arm would ache before the call even ended.

"I'm doing homework on it," Marcus said, tilting his own screen. "We're supposed to write two paragraphs on a monarchy, any one we pick."

Tyler opened the phone and found the little icon for the web. His parents had made one rule before the bus came: they would permit twenty minutes a day, and they could see the report that showed how much he used. The problem was that this morning the report already said nine minutes, and he had used it for maybe four. Something invisible was eating the time, and he wanted to know what.

He had a theory. Yesterday, while he was figuring the phone out, he had opened a weather app and a game and a music app, and he suspected they were still running in the background even after he closed them, like faucets left dripping. So he tested it. He found each app in the list and swiped it away, all of them, until the screen showed nothing running. Then he locked the phone, set it face down on his knee, and watched the second hand on his watch go around.

At the next pothole the bus jolted and the phone bounced an inch off his leg. He caught it, checked the screen, and opened the report. Still twenty minutes left, all twenty, no seconds ticking away.

"See?" he said, and held it up for Marcus. "It stopped."

The gate of Fairview Cemetery had an abrupt squeak that William heard from fifty feet away, which meant his little sister Ruthie was already inside. He found her standing between two graves, one with a stone cross carved with lilies, the other with a flat marker bearing a Star of David and small pebbles left by visitors. Their grandfather David was under the second one, and their great-aunt Maria was under the first, and William had been arguing with himself all week about which of them, if either, could still somehow see him standing there.

"It's not a contest," his mother had said at breakfast, but William had turned it into one anyway. Aunt Maria's church had taught that souls rise to heaven, whole and awake. Grandpa's synagogue taught something quieter, something William had never quite pinned down, and that was the problem. He had decided the way he decided things in science class: if two ideas explained the same thing differently, look for evidence, or at least for a test. His test was simple, if a little strange. He would stand at each grave and try saying something out loud, something he would only say if he thought someone was listening.

At Aunt Maria's cross he stood a long minute, then said, "I got moved up to second violin." Nothing happened, obviously, and he felt foolish in the hot still air. At Grandpa's marker he was about to repeat it when Ruthie held up a braided candle with several wicks, the one from the spice box their mom kept in the car for Saturday nights. "Mom says I'm allowed to hold the Havdalah candle this week," Ruthie said. "For the first time. And we still have the cup of grape juice and the spices to smell in the bag."

"You brought the whole thing here?" William asked.

"Grandpa would want to smell the spices," Ruthie said, as if that settled it, and William found he could not argue, because in his head the whole ceremony suddenly orbited the idea of separation, the Sabbath ending and the ordinary week beginning, one thing passing into another, the way a conductor lifts a hand and the music shifts into something you didn't expect.

He stood at the marker and changed his test. Instead of speaking as if to someone above, he said, "I got moved up to second violin, and I'm sorry I quit orchestra last year. That was a mistake." The words felt different than they had at the cross, less like sending a message and more like putting a pebble on the stone, which was something he'd always thought was just tradition. Maybe the two graves weren't competing after all. Maybe they were both pointing at something nobody could check from where they stood.

Ruthie tugged his sleeve. "You can hold the candle too," she said, "but only one wick end each."

Violet sat at the end of the lakeside dock with her duffel bag squashed behind her knees, waiting for the camp bus. The bus came at noon, her father had said twice, and it was already 11:40. She pressed her palm flat against the warm boards and thought about the fire last night in the backyard, the one she had talked him into. Marshmallows, then water from the hose, then bed. She had not stirred it. She had not checked anything. Somewhere in her stomach the memory sat like a stone.

When the bus arrived, a counselor named Renata climbed out and counted heads. "Cabin Four, we make one stop before check-in," she announced. "Yesterday's group left a fire ring by the shore. We make sure it's dead before we swim or cook or do anything else, and we do it fast. Swim check is at one."

The fire ring was a circle of black stones with a heap of gray ash in the middle. A boy named Declan poked a stick at it. "It's out. It's just ash." He kicked some aside and pale flakes drifted down like dirty snow. Violet crouched and looked closer. The ash was not lying loose the way cold powder would. It was stuck together in crusts, as if something underneath had baked it into a shell, and on the upwind side the crust was thicker. That was a pattern. Something she could not see had made it.

"Renata," Violet said. "Yesterday's group watered it, probably. But look, the ash is compressed into chunks. Can I try something?" Renata handed her the metal rake. Violet broke the crust open, and a red thread glowed inside like a worm hiding in a rotten apple. The others went quiet. "It's not out at all," she said, and her stomach turned as she pictured her own backyard, the hose, the sleeping neighborhood. "My dad taught me you have to drown it, stir it, drown it again, and then feel for heat. If a fire's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

They worked through lunch. Declan hauled the lake water in buckets with vigorous, splashy swings that soaked his sneakers, and Violet stirred until her arms ached, drowning each glowing pocket they uncovered. Renata pointed at the half-burned log and said the boring parts still mattered, since fungus and beetles were decomposers and even the black crumbs fed the soil, so they left the true ash in the ring and only took the danger out. Twice more Violet found hidden heat, once under a stone that had rolled over a coal. The second time, it took her a moment to believe it.

Finally she pulled her sleeve over her hand and pressed it to the middle of the drowned ash. Cool. She pressed every stone, every edge, all the way around, while Declan watched the trail for the swim check. "Cold," she reported. Renata checked behind her, then blew one long whistle blast toward the waterfront.

"Go get your suits," she said. "And Violet, you get the first off the dock."

Gabriella held the phone box on her lap all the way to the mall, tracing the picture of the phone on the lid with one finger. Her mother had one condition: prove she could handle it, and the phone stayed hers. The test started the moment they walked through the sliding doors.

"Meet me at the food court at four o'clock," her mother said, handing over the phone, already set up. "I'll be in the bookstore. If anything goes wrong, call me. That's the principle of the whole thing. A phone is for reaching people."

Gabriella agreed, but she was already distracted, because her best friend Priya was supposed to meet her at the fountain at three thirty, and Priya's mother had asked Gabriella to text when they found each other. That was her first real job with the phone. She wandered past the shoe stores, practicing, and sent Priya three texts full of exclamation points. Then she sat on the fountain's cool marble edge and waited.

Priya showed up at ten after, and they took turns taking ridiculous photos of each other with the giant plastic flamingo outside the candy shop. Then they bought pretzels and tried the game where you tilt the phone to steer a cart through a fruit stand. Gabriella noticed the battery draining fast and found a setting that seemed to save power. She tapped it on without reading carefully. After that, the afternoon blurred into window shopping, and when they finally parted at the escalator, Gabriella checked her messages to text Priya's mother. The message refused to send. She tried again. Nothing. A cold feeling crept up her neck.

At the food court, her mother was already waiting at a table, arms crossed, phone in hand. "I've been calling you for twenty minutes," she said. "Priya's mother called me in a panic because she never got your text. Where have you been?"

Gabriella's mouth went dry. "Right here. My phone just stopped sending things. I didn't do anything." Then she looked at the screen again, at the little airplane symbol in the corner, the one that had appeared right when she tapped the power-saving setting. She thought about how the phone had gone completely quiet, not one message coming in all afternoon, not even the group chat that never stopped buzzing. "Wait," she said slowly. "Airplane mode. It turns off the phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts." She tapped it off. The screen exploded with notifications, missed calls, texts stacking up one after another.

Her mother watched the messages pile in, then held out her hand for the phone. For a long moment neither of them spoke. "You figured it out yourself," her mother said finally. "That's something. But you put the phone in that mode without knowing what it did, and you didn't check it when things went quiet." Gabriella looked down at the tiny airplane still glowing faintly on the screen before it faded away.

"Can I keep it?" she asked.

Her mother slid the phone back across the table toward her.

The party was in Jayla's backyard, where a strip of grass near the fence had gone arid and brown from the summer heat and the rest was worn flat by feet. Twelve kids circled a folding table set up for the plane contest. Each person launched a rubber-band-powered balsa plane, and whoever's plane stayed in the air longest won the giant chocolate bar. Eli's plane had a bright red propeller that he had wound himself, twisting the band in careful half turns, and it had already outflown everyone on the first round.

Matthew had watched Eli wind that propeller at school too, in the corner of the cafeteria where Eli always sat alone. Some kids called him "Windup" and mimicked his careful, repetitive hand movements. Matthew had laughed once, in September, before he really knew Eli. He had been thinking about that laugh all week, the way you keep poking a sore tooth.

"Second round," Jayla announced. "Same rules as before." Eli rewound his plane. It climbed, stalled, and drifted down so slowly it seemed to change its mind about landing. It beat the next three planes easily.

"We should change it," said Dylan, who had been loud about everything all afternoon. "Longest distance should count, not longest time. Time rewards planes that just float around doing nothing." His eyes flicked toward Eli, and the look conveyed exactly what he meant, even though he never said Eli's name.

A couple of kids nodded. Eli's shoulders drew in, and he started putting his plane back in its box, the cardboard closing over the red propeller like a lid over something embarrassing. Matthew felt the September laugh rise in his own throat, and this time he recognized it for what it was.

"Wait," Matthew said. His voice came out louder than he expected, and everyone turned. "Last summer at camp we changed a rule like that, halfway through a game, and the guy who suggested it won. I didn't say anything then. I just thought it was bad luck." He picked up Eli's box and set it back on the table, keeping it open. "Here's what I figured out. Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them." He looked at Dylan. "You already know distance helps your plane. That's why you thought of it now."

Dylan's mouth opened, then closed. "It was just an idea," he muttered.

"Then suggest it before the next game," Jayla said. "We'll all vote when nobody knows who it helps. Eli, you're up for the final round."

Eli rewound the propeller, his hands steadier than before, and launched. The plane rode a breeze coming over the fence, circled the arid strip of grass twice, and came down past everyone else's marks. "Sixteen seconds," Jayla called. Eli allowed himself a small, quick smile, and Matthew found he was smiling too.

"Alright," Dylan said, pulling his own plane from his backpack. "Before the next game starts, I have a rule to propose."

Joshua stood in the drama room with his arms crossed, staring at his partner, Devon, who had just pretended to hand him a pizza. "No, it's not a pizza, it's a hat," Joshua said, and Devon groaned. Ms. Reyes clapped her hands and told the class to freeze, then walked to the shelf and pulled down a book so worn its cover was soft at the corners. She dropped it on Joshua's desk on her way past. "Spolin, 1963," she said. "Look it up tonight. And play the game right tomorrow."

At home, Joshua flipped through the book, Improvisation for the Theater, finding pages of games with names like "Mirror" and "Where." His mom leaned over his shoulder. "Ms. Reyes says people call it the bible of improv teaching," Joshua told her. "It collected all these theater games together, back in 1963." He kept reading, and one phrase kept appearing: accept the offer. When your partner hands you a pizza, the pizza is real because you both agree it is. Joshua wondered if that was the hidden rule behind the whole book, the pattern underneath every game. How could he test it?

The next day he decided to invest one full class period in a simple experiment: say yes to every single offer Devon made, no matter how strange, and add something new to it. Devon started the scene as an astronaut. "Yes, and the spaceship is out of fuel," Joshua said. Devon's eyebrows went up, then he leaned in. "Yes, and the fuel we need is peanut butter." "Yes, and it has to be nutritious peanut butter, for the long flight." They built a whole mission out of nothing, one agreement stacked on another, until Devon declared the spaceship had landed on a planet ruled by houseplants.

Afterward Joshua noticed something odd. When he had blocked Devon's pizza, the scene had died in seconds, like a pond going stagnant. When they kept saying yes, the scene grew, like an ecosystem where everything fed something else. He hadn't seen that rule written anywhere on one page, but it was there under all the games, holding them up.

On Friday Ms. Reyes had them perform in front of the class. Halfway through their scene, Devon grabbed an invisible microphone and said, "Breaking news, everyone, the mayor is a giant squid." Joshua felt the old reflex rise, the urge to say no, that's silly. Instead he took the microphone and turned to the class.

"Yes, and I have an exclusive interview with him right now."

The Saturday maths clinic at the community centre met in a room with a foosball table nobody was allowed to touch, which struck Bentley as eccentric, since the centre had put it there in the first place. He spread out his worksheet at a wobbly table by the window. At the top, in his teacher's handwriting, was the problem: prove the two triangles congruent by side-angle-side, then show that the third sides are equal without measuring them.

Bentley could do the first part. He had drawn both triangles side by side, marked off two matching sides and the angle squeezed between them, and written his statement in the careful three-column format his teacher demanded. Side, angle, side. SAS. Done. It was the second part that annoyed him. Without measuring. His ruler sat right there in his pencil case, and someone had told him not to use it, which made him want to use it very badly.

Across the table, Priya was building a tower out of borrowing slips. She glanced at his paper. "You've proved they're congruent," she said. "So?"

"So now I have to prove the last sides match, and I'm not allowed to measure."

"That's the whole point, though, isn't it?" Priya dropped a slip on her tower. "If you've proved the triangles are exactly the same triangle, then the rest of it comes free."

Bentley frowned at his drawing. He tried an experiment. He traced triangle one onto tracing paper, then slid it over triangle two. It landed perfectly, corner on corner, line on line. The triangles were the same shape, the same size, identical in every part. He hadn't measured the third side. He hadn't needed to. Once the triangles matched, everything in them matched, including the one side he cared about. There was a principle at work here, and he was fairly sure it had a name, because everything in this unit had a name.

He checked the back page of his textbook, where the glossary lived. CPCTC. He said it out loud once, like a sneeze. "Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent," he read, and under that he wrote the five letters in the reason column of his proof. His teacher would like that. His teacher liked reasons more than answers.

Priya leaned over. "CPCTC," she read off his page. "Sounds like a band nobody's heard of."

"It's better than measuring," Bentley said. "You prove three things, and you get the fourth one for nothing." He looked at the worksheet again, then at the three problems below it, the ones he'd been dreading. Each of them wanted the same trick: prove two triangles congruent first, then use that to drag out whatever else you needed. He began to devise a plan for problem four, which had triangles hiding inside a bigger triangle, like a puzzle inside a puzzle. Find the matching sides and angle. Write SAS. Then let CPCTC carry the rest of the weight.

He worked through the remaining problems while Priya's tower of borrowing slips grew steadily less stable beside him. On the last problem, the two triangles shared a side, and he realized the shared side counted as a matching side all by itself, one less line to write. He underlined his final CPCTC, closed his workbook, and, on his way out, gave the foosball table a slow, respectful spin.

The waiting room of the veterinary clinic smelled like dog shampoo and coffee, and Asher spread his homework across two chairs while his terrier mix, Biscuit, waited for her shots. His assignment was due tomorrow: explain how finches on different islands ended up with different beak shapes, and why. He had a bag of birdseed and a pile of tweezers, pliers, and chopsticks from the kitchen drawer, because he had a plan. If he was going to understand natural selection, he wanted to see it happen in front of him.

He dumped two kinds of seed on a paper tray. Sunflower seeds sat whole and hard, and a pile of tiny millet grains scattered like sand. "Biscuit," he said, holding up the pliers, "you're a big-beaked finch." Biscuit wagged. Asher used the pliers to crack a sunflower seed in four seconds, then tried to pick up a single millet grain and chased it across the tray until it shot onto the floor. The tweezers grabbed millet instantly but squeezed the sunflower seed uselessly, like biting a rock with a straw. He wrote the times down, grinning. Tools matched to food. That was the whole game.

A boy about his age sat across from him with a rabbit carrier and watched the whole seed chase. "Why are you doing that in a vet's office?" the boy asked. Asher told him: on islands with hard seeds, birds whose beaks could crack them survived and had chicks with those beaks, and over many generations the whole island ended up with thick beaks. On islands with small soft seeds, the opposite happened. "Nobody planned it," Asher said. "The food did the choosing." The boy nodded slowly, like the idea had finally clicked into place.

Then the boy squinted at Asher's notebook, where Asher had scribbled a messy timeline from the science museum field trip last week. "That part's wrong," the boy said. "You wrote that animals were declared to be made of cells first." Asher looked. He had guessed animals came first because animals seemed more complicated and more important, so surely scientists studied them first. But at the museum he had stood in front of the timeline wall for ten whole minutes, and now he remembered. "No, wait," Asher said, flipping his notes over. "In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells. Plants came first, and animals came after." The boy changed his mind about the notebook being useless and pulled out his phone to double-check, and it matched. Plants had gotten the cell theory jury's first verdict, a whole year before anyone said it about animals.

"Your old guess is obsolete," the boy said, and Asher laughed and crossed it out. A seed had to fit a beak, and a fact had to fit the evidence, and his guess hadn't fit either one. When the tech called Biscuit's name, Asher swept the seeds into his bag, thinking he'd nurture the finch idea into a full report tonight. Biscuit trotted through the door ahead of him, nose down, hunting crumbs off the floor.

Lucy stood at the long steel counter of the community kitchen, staring at three recipes she had copied onto one index card. The windows looked out over the estuary, where the river fanned out wide and brown before it met the gray sea. She liked watching the two waters slide past each other without mixing, but today she had a bigger puzzle: rice, curry, and flatbread all needed to be done at the same moment, and each one took a different number of minutes.

"If the rice takes twenty and the flatbread takes two per piece," she said to her friend Dara, ticking numbers with her pencil, "then flatbread has to go last. But the curry has to simmer for fifteen. When do I start?" Dara shrugged and kept kneading her own dough. Lucy decided she could deduce the answer by working backward from the end. If everything should be ready at noon, the rice went on the stove first, then the curry, then the flatbread, one piece at a time, straight onto the hot pan.

She started the rice at eleven forty. While it absorbed its water, she chopped onions for the curry, her eyes streaming so much that Dara laughed and slid her a pair of swimming goggles from the lost-and-found box. "You look exceptional," Dara said, and Lucy grinned behind the foggy lenses and kept chopping.

The curry went into the pot at eleven forty-five, and Lucy stirred it and thought about a dinner she'd had at Dara's house last month. Dara's mother had made a smooth white sauce, flour and butter in the pan first, then milk poured in slowly while she whisked. It had turned silky and thick, nothing like the lumpy glue Lucy once made at home. She had been wondering about it ever since. "What did your mom call that white sauce?" she asked.

"Béchamel," Dara said. "A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking." Lucy rolled the word around. Mother sauce. As if all the other sauces were its children, the way the estuary outside fed a hundred little channels. She wondered what else in cooking had a family tree, and whether the curry bubbling in front of her belonged to one too.

At eleven fifty-five the rice was resting, the curry was simmering on low, and Lucy divided her dough into balls and rolled the first one thin. It hit the pan and puffed up in the middle like a small balloon, and she flipped it and watched it brown in spots. One by one the flatbreads stacked on a plate under a towel. At noon exactly, she looked around her. Rice, steaming. Curry, thick enough to coat the spoon. Flatbread, warm and stacked. Everything at once, like she had planned it, though her heart was still going quick.

They carried the pots to the long tables where the Saturday lunch crowd was already gathering, and Dara's mother found a seat near the window. Lucy ladled curry over rice and handed her a flatbread. "You made this?" Dara's mother asked, tearing off a piece.

"All three, ready at the same time," Lucy said. "I worked backward from noon. And tomorrow I want to make béchamel."

Jaxon stood at the kitchen table with a poster board, a bag of marbles, and his older cousin's phone number written on a sticky note. His health teacher had assigned him the hardest topic in the class: explain how nicotine hooks people, right down to the brain. He could not see a brain working, and that was the problem. He had to narrate something invisible to a room full of seventh graders, and he wanted it to be good.

"Got a minute?" he said when his cousin Dre picked up. Dre had quit vaping last spring, and Jaxon had been meaning to ask him about it for a week. Dre talked while Jaxon spread the marbles across the table like a handful of random pebbles. "It wasn't one big decision," Dre said. "It crept in. Good feeling first, then needing it just to feel normal." Jaxon pushed a marble along a track he had drawn on the poster, a curve labeled REWARD PATHWAY, and watched where it rolled.

Later that afternoon his little sister Riya came in from her checkup and dropped her jacket on a chair. She was quiet in a way Jaxon recognized, because two years ago he had sat in that same beige exam room, in that same squeaky chair, and asked Dr. Okafor why every other boy in gym class seemed to be changing and he wasn't. He remembered staring at the paper on the wall while the doctor talked, too embarrassed to look up. He remembered exactly what it said, too, because he had read it four times.

"Everything okay?" he asked Riya now. She shrugged. "I asked the doctor if something was wrong with me because I haven't started yet, and Ava already has." Jaxon told her what the wall chart had told him, the thing he had tested in his own head that day in the exam room. "Puberty usually starts between ages eight and thirteen for girls and between nine and fourteen for boys," he said, laying out the marbles into two rows, one shorter, one longer, the way he had pictured it back then. "So girls can start as early as eight, boys as early as nine, and starting anywhere in those ranges is normal. You and me, we're both inside the lines." Riya picked up a marble from the girls' row and held it to the light. "So Ava just started early," she said, "and I'm not late at all."

Jaxon looked at his rows of marbles, then at the curving track on his poster, and smiled. Ranges and pathways, both invisible, both working quietly whether anyone saw them or not. For his presentation he would roll one marble down the track for the first cigarette, then a handful for the tenth, showing how nicotine kept hitting the reward pathway until the brain expected it, the way Dre had described. Riya set her marble back in its row. "Can I watch you practice after dinner?" she asked. Jaxon picked up the bag and shook it, listening to the click inside. "Sure," he said. "You can be the audience."

The community pool at nine in the morning was almost empty, which was exactly why Beatrice had claimed lane two for her secret project: learning to pace an eight-hundred-metre race even though she was standing in three feet of chlorinated water. Her plan, hatched last night with a notebook and two markers, was to walk one pool length fast, then walk a second length immediately, and feel the difference between starting too fast and starting right.

"Move over, you're invading my coaching zone," said a voice from the fence. It was Dominic from her grade, dragging five plastic hurdles onto the grass beside the pool. He wanted to make the county hurdles team more than he wanted lunch, probably, because he'd been out there every morning all week, crashing into the same hurdle and swearing in a way he thought nobody could hear.

"Why don't you just ask Coach to move them?" Beatrice called through the fence.

"He'd say I'm not ready for race spacing." Dominic wiped sweat off his forehead. "But I asked him yesterday anyway, and guess what. He said yes, backwards." He yanked the first hurdle closer to the second and clicked it down to its lowest notch. "We learn the three-step rhythm with hurdles lower and closer together than race spacing. Then we move them apart as we get faster. So today they're short and squished and I only have to survive."

Beatrice stood in the water with her mouth open. Shorter and closer first. Start with the small version of the thing, then grow it. She thought of last Tuesday's time trial, when she'd exploded off the line, led the whole first lap, and then her legs had turned to something molten, like her muscles had melted inside her skin, and three girls had passed her before the final curve. Her coach had said "save something," which had meant nothing to her at the time, like being told to save money when you couldn't see the money.

But pacing was a thing you couldn't see, and that was the problem. Speed you could see. Energy left in your legs, you could not. So maybe, like Dominic's hurdles, she needed the squished-together version. She set her goggles, pushed off, and swam one length flat-out, then tried to immediately swim a second. Halfway down the return lap her arms felt like wet noodles and she had to grab the lane rope, gasping, while a lifeguard gave her the look you give a drowning hamster. Okay. That was the "too fast first lap," demonstrated in a place where she could stop and think about it instead of collapsing on a track in front of everyone.

Second attempt. She counted her strokes on the first length, deliberately holding back, and it felt almost boring, like walking when you wanted to run. Then the second length, and her arms still worked, still pulled, and she touched the wall breathing hard but whole. Through the fence, Dominic cleared all five low hurdles in a row without touching one, and threw his arms up like he'd won the Olympics.

"Did you see that?" he shouted.

"I saw it," Beatrice called back, grinning into her goggles. "Now move them apart."

The cardboard box on the passenger seat tipped sideways twice on the drive home, and each time Alyssa's hand shot out to steady it. Inside, tangled in an old flannel shirt, was a six-month-old mutt from the shelter, brown with one white ear, whom she had named Biscuit an hour after meeting him. Her mother kept her eyes on the road and said, "He's your responsibility, you know. Food, walks, everything." Alyssa nodded, though she was barely listening. She was busy wondering what he was thinking behind those wide brown eyes, and whether a dog could miss a place he'd only lived in for six weeks.

That first evening, Biscuit explored the kitchen like a detective, nose down, tail up. Alyssa followed him, cataloguing his discoveries. He was curious about the refrigerator, terrified of the ceiling fan, and completely fascinated by the space under the couch, where he stayed for ten full minutes. When her friend Priya knocked on the door, Alyssa grabbed the bag of trail mix she'd been saving and Biscuit trotted after her into the backyard.

They sat on the porch steps, and Biscuit sat too, staring at the bag with an intensity that made Alyssa laugh. She picked out a raisin and held it out. "Want a treat?"

"Stop!" Priya's hand shot across, almost knocking the raisin into the grass. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs. They should never be given as treats."

Alyssa froze with her hand in the air. "Seriously? They're just dried grapes."
