"Seriously. My aunt's a vet tech. It's one of the first things she told me."

Alyssa looked at the raisin, then at Biscuit, who was drooling hopefully. A cold thought slid into her mind. The bag of trail mix had been sitting on the coffee table all afternoon, and the zipper had looked open when she picked it up. She tried to interpret the evidence calmly, the way detectives did in the books she liked. An open bag, a dog alone in the living room for hours, a dog who adored nosing under furniture and into things. She couldn't see what had happened while she was in her room. But she could test it.

She carried the bag to the kitchen table and counted. Yesterday there had been a big clump of raisins stuck together at the bottom; she remembered picking around them because she liked the almonds best. Now the bottom of the bag held only almonds, peanuts, and two chocolate chips. The raisins were gone. Every single one.

"Mom!" Her voice came out higher than she intended. "Biscuit ate raisins. A lot of them, I think. From the trail mix."

Her mother appeared in the doorway, dish towel over her shoulder, and studied the bag. Then she was already dialing the animal clinic, giving Biscuit's weight and the approximate number of raisins, while Alyssa knelt beside the dog and ran her hands over his warm sides, feeling for anything wrong. There was nothing to feel, of course. Whatever was happening inside him was hidden, and the probability that he was fine felt, to Alyssa, like a coin she couldn't see. The vet's voice crackled through the phone, calm and steady, and her mother said, "Bring him in now."

Alyssa had a sudden flashback to the shelter that morning, the moment Biscuit had pressed his nose against her palm through the bars of the kennel, deciding something about her in a single sniff. Now she scooped him into the cardboard box, flannel shirt and all, and held the box on her lap in the back seat the whole way there. Somewhere outside, the streetlights were flickering on, and a raccoon she'd watched raid the trash cans all summer, strictly nocturnal, was just beginning to stir. Biscuit burrowed deeper into the shirt and let out a small, uncertain whine.

"Almost there," Alyssa whispered. "And after tonight, no more raisins. Ever. Deal?"

The train from upstate pulled into the dilapidated platform fifteen minutes late, and Grandpa Ray stepped down carrying one battered suitcase and a paper bag of maple candies. Vincent had been waiting for an hour, holding a sign he'd made that said WELCOME GRANDPA in marker. He waved it so hard the paper tore at the corner.

"I thought we'd lose you to that delay," Vincent said, grabbing the suitcase handle.

"Trains run when trains run," Grandpa said. "No use opposing it. Where's your mother's car?" On the way home, Vincent noticed Grandpa hadn't touched the water bottle Mom had packed, and he noticed it again at dinner, and again the next morning when the orange juice sat untouched beside Grandpa's plate.

On Tuesday they went to the park, and it was the hottest day of the week so far. Grandpa sat on a bench in the shade while Vincent did three trips across the monkey bars. When Vincent came back, dripping, Grandpa's face was flushed and his eyes looked heavy, but he said he was fine. Vincent fetched two waters from the fountain anyway and pressed one into his grandfather's hand. "You haven't had anything to drink since breakfast," he said. "I've been counting."

"I'd tell you if I were thirsty," Grandpa said, but he drank the whole bottle, and then a second one Vincent brought back. Ten minutes later he sat up straighter and said the bench felt cooler, which it didn't, because the sun hadn't moved. Vincent made an inference from that: something was off in Grandpa's own alarm system, not in the day itself. He called his mom at work and asked one careful question, and she said yes, the body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without ever feeling thirsty. Vincent hung up and made a decision on the spot.

For the rest of the week, he carried a water bottle everywhere and refilled Grandpa's glass at every meal without being asked, and he set a timer on his watch that buzzed every hour. Grandpa grumbled about being managed, but by Friday he was walking the whole loop around the pond without stopping, planning to teach Vincent chess that evening and to beat him, he claimed, in under twenty moves.

On Saturday morning, back at the same train station, Grandpa handed Vincent a fresh bottle of water before boarding. "For the walk home," he said. "You've got the habit now. Keep it." Then he stepped up onto the train, and Vincent stood holding the cold bottle until the last car disappeared around the curve.

The pitch counter app on Coach Alvarez's phone was still a prototype, a rough version his brother had built, and it glitched whenever someone's shadow crossed the screen. Brooklyn had volunteered to keep count on a clipboard instead, because she liked numbers better than surprises. She sat on the bench behind third base, marking every pitch Marcus threw, and by the fourth inning she had a funny feeling in her stomach. According to her sheet, Marcus had thrown sixty-one pitches. According to the coach's phone, he had thrown forty-four.

"Coach," she said quietly, jogging over between batters, "the app might be missing some. It freezes when it's sunny, and it was sunny all inning." She showed him her clipboard, where she had also noted which warmup tosses she had counted and which she had left out, so he could check her reasoning himself.

Coach Alvarez looked at the numbers, then at Marcus on the mound, then called time. He walked out, put a hand on the boy's shoulder, and led him back to the bench. "You're done for today, bud. You hit your pitch limit."

Marcus dropped his glove in the dust. "I don't even feel tired."

"That's not what the limit is about," Coach said. Brooklyn expected a lecture, but he just sat down next to Marcus and rubbed his own elbow like an old memory lived there.

Marcus stared at the dirt. "My cousin plays high school ball and throws a hundred pitches a game."

"That's because his bones finished growing," Marcus's older sister, Delia, called from the fence. She was a sophomore and had driven him to practice. "Yours haven't. You've still got growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of your bones. They're weaker than the bone around them, so young pitchers have limits on how much stress we can put on them." She shrugged. "I learned it in health class after I wrecked my shoulder swimming."

Brooklyn wrote that down too, in the margin, because it suddenly made everything make sense. The limits weren't about being tired. They were about something you couldn't see, working quietly inside a person's arm, and the pitch count was the only way to see it from the outside. She decided to test her idea. She flipped back through her sheets from the last three games and found that Marcus had also been participating in every throwing drill at every practice, on top of his games. When she showed him the tally, his face changed.

"Okay," he said. "Maybe I'll catch on drill days."

He picked up his glove, walked over to the cooler, and came back with two cups of water, handing one to Brooklyn before he sat down to watch the rest of the inning.

The graph in George's lap was supposed to keep him busy until Flagstaff, but it had turned into an argument instead. He had printed two rainfall charts at the library before the trip, one for the Sonoran Desert and one for the Hoh Rainforest in Washington, and his older sister, Priya, riding shotgun, kept glancing back at him instead of the map. "You're going to wrinkle the airport," she said, meaning the fold where the Sonoran bar column looked like a row of flat pennies. The Hoh's bars were tall blue towers, some of them taller than George's thumb.

"Look at this," George said, holding the sheets up. "The desert gets barely anything. Like, the whole year is shorter than one rainforest month." Priya's stomach rumbled audibly from the front seat, and Dad took the next exit toward a diner with a gravel lot and a sign shaped like a saguaro. Outside the window the actual desert slid past, all rust and pale green, smelling of hot dust through the cracked vent.

At the diner, the waitress refilled their waters and noticed the graphs spread across the table next to the ketchup. "Homework on vacation," she said, and George felt his ears go warm, because the graphs had been his own idea. Last summer he had refused to do the workbook pages Mom bought him, and she had ended up donating the whole thing, which he still thought about sometimes without deciding whether he'd been right. "What are you comparing?" the waitress asked.

"Rainfall," George said. "A desert is a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. Ten inches." He tapped the Sonoran sheet. "That's how scientists define it, not just sand and heat."

The waitress laughed and set down a basket of fries. "Then you know what's funny? Where I grew up, in Antarctica's dry valleys, they call that a desert too. Cold one. Snow barely falls there at all." George stared at her. Snow. A desert. Priya pulled out her phone and started reading, and for ten minutes the only sounds were ice clinking and the fryer humming behind the counter.

Back in the car, George took out a fresh index card and drew a temperature graph next to the rainfall bars, the Hoh's line mild and level, the Sonoran's line a jagged climb. The two places were opposites in every way except that both had living things that had found a way. He thought about the estuary they had visited on the Oregon coast last spring, where the river met the sea and everything depended on the balance of fresh and salt, and how his class's influential poster about it had won the hall contest even though it had almost no numbers on it. Numbers mattered, he decided, pushing the pen harder. He would add Antarctica to the card, a cold desert with a line that dove below zero while rainfall stayed under ten inches. "When we hit Washington," he told Priya, "I'm going to stand in the rain and measure it."

"You'll need a bigger cup," she said.

Clara spread the two flowcharts across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the corners with jars of homemade pickles. The assignment was due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, put it in her own words, and explain it to the class. But her teacher had also promised bonus marks for describing how a bill becomes a law, and Clara had never gotten that far before.

"Still working on the homework?" her grandfather asked, setting down two mugs of tea. He was a veteran who had served overseas decades ago, and he kept a framed photograph of his old regiment in the hallway. "You've been at that table all afternoon."

"I picked section two," Clara said. "Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression. My own words for it are: you're allowed to think what you think and say what you think, without the government stopping you." She frowned at the flowcharts. "But I'm stuck on the bill part. The federal chart says a bill goes through the House of Commons and then the Senate, and then the Governor General gives royal assent. The provincial chart just stops after one box."

Last weekend, she remembered, she had complained that the assignment was pointless. She had wanted to quit and write about her weekend instead, and her grandfather had said, "People obstruct laws they've never read, Clara. Read this one." Then he had slid a worn booklet across this same table, and she had opened it just to be polite. The first line had caught her before she could pretend to be bored.

Now she traced the provincial chart with her finger. "That can't be right. Every law should have to pass both houses. Otherwise it's too easy to pass something bad."

"Draw it again," her grandfather said. "Count the boxes yourself. Don't trust the chart."

Clara counted. The federal chart showed two chambers, first one and then the other, before the Governor General. The provincial chart showed one chamber only, and after that single chamber the bill went straight to the lieutenant governor, who gave royal assent. She checked the provincial government website on her laptop, then checked a second site because she was skeptical of anything she found only once. Both said the same thing.

"Grandpa, look. All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures. So a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent." She said it slowly, testing each word. "That's why the chart isn't missing anything. It's just shorter."

"So will you change your mind about the shorter chart?" he asked.

"It's not wrong, it's just different," Clara said. She was thinking of the boy in her class, Daniel, who had insisted last week that provincial laws took twice as long to pass as federal ones because there were more provinces. She had believed him then. Now she had a page of counted boxes that said otherwise, and she intended to wave it at him on Monday.

She copied the two flowcharts side by side onto a fresh sheet, wrote "one house, not two" beside the provincial one, and underlined it twice.

"There," she said. "Now for section two."

Megan sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with the laptop open and a deadline hanging over her: the student council meeting was at four o'clock, and she had promised to bring a summary of the field trip survey. Grandpa hovered behind her with his own want, which was to get the kitchen back for his bread baking before the dough overproofed.

"Five minutes," she negotiated, tilting the screen away from his flour-dusted elbow.

The spreadsheet held 212 rows, one for each student who had answered the survey. There was a column for grade, a column for the activity they chose, and a column where everyone rated the trip from one to five. Megan had figured out pivot tables the night before, mostly by clicking things at random until a gray panel appeared and dragged fields into boxes. She put Grade in Rows, and the count of students appeared neatly for each grade. Sixth grade, 74. Seventh, 68. Eighth, 70.

But the count told her nothing about whether anyone had actually liked the trip. She scrolled through the ratings and saw a wall of threes, fours, ones, and fives with no order she could detect. There had to be a pattern in there somewhere, a rule hiding inside the numbers, but it was invisible while the ratings sat scattered down the column.

She clicked into the values area of the pivot table and found a dropdown. Sum was selected, which made no sense; summing ratings would just give giant useless numbers. She changed it to Count, which she already had. Then she saw Average. That had to be it. The whole column of one-to-five ratings would turn into the mean rating for each grade. She clicked it and the table rebuilt itself. Sixth grade, 4.2. Seventh, 3.1. Eighth, 4.6. She sat back. The eighth graders had loved the trip, the seventh graders had barely tolerated it, and now she could say so with actual numbers instead of a shrug.

Megan tested it once to be sure, dragging the Activity field into Columns so the average rating showed for each activity within each grade. The pattern held: seventh graders who chose the museum averaged 4.4, while the ones stuck with the walking tour averaged 2.3. The tour was the problem. That was worth saying at the meeting, and she could even propose fixing it for next year.

"Done," she said, and slid the laptop aside as Grandpa slid the loaf pan in. "Grandpa, you're my spreadsheet mentor now, by default."

"Only if mentoring means standing here eating bread," he said, and set a warm slice in front of her.

Sophie wanted to win the school science fair more than she wanted her braces off, and she had decided the way to do it was to settle, once and for all, which classroom surface had the most bacteria. Mr. Ruiz had given each table four agar plates, and Sophie's table got the pencil sharpener, the doorknob, the sink faucet, and the teacher's keyboard. "You can't see bacteria," said her lab partner, Marcus, peering at his plate. "So how do we know the shiny stuff isn't just soup?" Sophie pointed at the dots already blooming on the plate they had swabbed that morning. "We can't see them, but we can see what they do. That's the whole trick."

While they waited for colonies to grow, Marcus flipped through a magazine and held up a page. "Look at this ad. Germ-Away wipes change lives," he read. "Wow. Changes lives." Sophie squinted at it. "Fine, but how would you check that?" Marcus shrugged. "You'd have to find a bunch of lives, wipe them, and see." The table cracked up, and even Priya from the next table leaned over to see what was so funny.

Sophie couldn't stop thinking about it, though. She took out her notebook and wrote two columns. In one she put claims like "Germ-Away kills more bacteria than plain soap," which she underlined twice, because Mr. Ruiz had a bottle of each and a whole drawer of plates. You could swab, wipe, wait, count. In the other column she put "changes lives," and after a minute she also put her mother's favorite, "these vitamins make you feel unstoppable," because she could not imagine any plate, anywhere, that could ever prove that wrong. It was like an opinion wearing a lab coat.

"The kill-more-bacteria one is checkable," she told Marcus. "The changes-lives one gives us nothing to test. Not even in principle, whatever principle means." "It means it just can't be done," Marcus said, "even if you had a million plates and a robot." Priya nodded solemnly. "My brother wrote an algorithm that sorts true facts from false ones for his homework," she offered, "and even his algorithm chokes on stuff like that."

Sophie had to confess something then. "I was going to put 'Germ-Away is the best' on my poster, because it sounds strong." Marcus pretended to faint against the sink. "Be strong and checkable," Sophie added, writing it at the top of her column, right under the date.

The next morning the plates had turned into tiny, fertile gardens, gray and orange colonies crowding the pencil sharpener's plate worst of all, which made everybody groan and nobody surprised. Mr. Ruiz stopped at their table and looked a long time at the notebook with its two columns and the circled words "nothing to test." He tapped the page. "Whose is this?" Sophie raised her hand, braced for trouble. He wrote something in his binder instead. "Sofia," he said, "remind me to show you what Karl Popper did with this idea. You'll like him. He was even crankier than you."

Sophie grinned. "That's an opinion, Mr. Ruiz."

"Checkable," he said, and moved on to the next table.

The restaurant smelled of ginger and scallions, and Claire's stomach growled before the waiter had even set down the menus. Mei's family owned the Golden Lantern, and tonight Mei's grandmother had insisted on cooking "something special," which turned out to be seven dishes that all seemed to revolve around one enormous pot of rice in the middle of the table. Claire wanted more than anything to make a good impression. Her plan was simple: eat everything, compliment everything, and not knock anything over.

The trouble started with the dumplings. They were slippery, and Claire needed both hands to fish one out of the shared platter. Without thinking, she planted her chopsticks straight up in her bowl of rice like two little flagpoles and reached across the table. The chatter around the table stopped. Mei's grandmother went very still, and her eyes flicked to the bowl and then quickly away, as if she had seen something she did not want to see.

"Nan, what's wrong?" Mei asked her grandmother in a low voice. Then Mei followed the old woman's gaze, and Claire watched her friend's face change from confusion to understanding. Mei leaned over and whispered, "Don't leave your chopsticks standing in the rice. It looks like incense offered to the dead." Claire pulled the chopsticks out so fast she nearly launched a grain of rice into the soy sauce. "Oh no. Oh no, I'm so sorry," she whispered back. Mei's grandmother said something in Chinese, and Mei laughed for the first time since the dumpling incident. "She says you have good reflexes. She once knocked over a whole teapot doing the same thing at her own grandmother's table."

Claire laid her chopsticks across the top of her bowl the way she saw everyone else do, resting them side by side like a pair of quiet birds. Then, because she wanted to be sure, she watched Mei's father closely through the next three courses. He never once left his chopsticks planted anywhere, not even when he answered his phone about some argument with the landlord over the leaking roof. Every time he needed a free hand, down the chopsticks went, flat beside the bowl. Claire tested her theory by pretending to need both hands for her napkin. Resting the chopsticks, she decided, was the safe pattern, the invisible rule that everyone at this table knew and she had just learned the hard way.

After dinner, Mei's grandmother pressed a small red envelope into Claire's hands. "For luck," Mei translated. "She likes you. She says anyone who apologizes that fast can come back anytime." At the door, Claire turned and held up the envelope with a grin. "Same time next month? I promise my chopsticks will lie down like well-trained puppies." Behind her, she heard Mei's grandmother laugh, a sound like small bells.

Mya sat cross-legged on her bed with her phone six inches from her face, watching the group chat light up. The project was due Friday: make a page about where your family came from. Jordan had already typed three messages about presenting first because he wanted the class to remember his slide before anyone else's, and Priya had sent a photo of her grandmother's cookbook. Mya hadn't sent anything yet, because she had a problem. Her cousin Lena was visiting from abroad, and last night at dinner Lena had laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass when everyone kept saying she'd flown in from Germany.

"It's Deutschland," Lena had said. "We never call it Germany. That's your word for us, not ours." Then she'd told Mya the names for the two kinds of words, and Mya had written them on the back of her math homework so she wouldn't forget.

She typed into the chat: "Hypothetical question. If we call a country one thing and the people there call it something else, which name should go on my poster?" Jordan answered fast: "Ours, obviously, it's for our class." Priya sent a shrug emoji. Mya tried a different approach, the way she'd test a rule in science: collect data. She messaged her uncle, her grandmother, and Lena's mother, asking each one what their family called the country in their own language.

The answers came in through the evening. Her grandmother wrote back a whole text about the village, and then added, "Here we say it our way, there they say it theirs, both are true names." Lena's mother sent one line: "Deutschland, always." Mya copied the messages into a document for her citation page, so her teacher could see where each name came from. She noticed a pattern: every family member used their own word, and not one of them used the English one, unless they were talking to someone outside.

"So which one wins?" Jordan asked, when she posted her draft. He still wanted his slide first and had moved on to arguing about presentation order, but Priya had gone quiet, and then sent: "Wait. My mom calls our family's country something different too. I just never thought about it. Can I put both on my page?"

Mya looked at Lena, who was leaning in the doorway in her borrowed sweatpants, reading over her shoulder. Lena tapped the screen where Mya had typed both names side by side, then the two labels underneath them. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," Lena said, "and a name outsiders use is an exonym." Mya added the last line to her poster and hit send. Priya replied within a minute: "Doing it. Mine's going up first, Jordan."

"Fine," Jordan typed. "But I'm still going before the bell invades my free time."

Hazel stood on the back porch of Marisol's birthday party holding a paper with six numbered lines on it, because tomorrow she had to run the first Nature Club meeting of the year and she had never run anything except a lemonade stand that failed. Marisol had offered her party as a practice audience. "Pretend we're the club," Marisol said, waving a forkful of cake at the six kids scattered around the porch. "You be the conductor."

"Conductor of what?" asked Theo.

"Of the meeting," Hazel said. "Like an orchestra, except with people who all want to talk about salamanders at once." She read the first line of her agenda. "Item one: does anyone actually want to sell candy at the fall fair, or was that just Mr. Ruiz's idea?" It went surprisingly well for two items. Priya argued, Dev made a joke about the treasurer's report, but everyone got a turn, and Hazel started to believe she could do this.

Then item three fell apart because of the laughing.

A boy named Quinn was standing near the snack table, and two kids from another school, Rex and some kid Hazel didn't know, were circling him. "Nice shoes," Rex kept saying. "No, really. Nice shoes." They said it in that voice that meant the opposite, and Quinn's ears went red, and every time Rex spoke, the second kid laughed like a drum machine.

Hazel's first idea was to say something sharp to Rex. She even opened her mouth. But then she noticed something she couldn't see directly, only its shadow: Rex kept glancing sideways before each joke, checking whether the porch was still watching. It was like watching a performer count his audience. The laughing kid was the audience. Take away the audience, she thought, and what's left?

She revised her plan mid-breath. "Quinn!" she called, loud and casual. "Come on, let's go. I need help with the snacks in the kitchen." Quinn blinked, then pushed off the table and followed her through the screen door. Rex opened his mouth for another "nice shoes," but there was nobody left to hear it except his one friend, and somehow that wasn't enough. When Hazel peeked back through the window thirty seconds later, Rex was standing there looking bizarre, like a magician whose trick had ended early, and then he wandered off toward the bounce house.

In the kitchen, Quinn dumped chips into a bowl without being asked. "Thanks," he said. "That was getting old."

"That's the whole trick, I think," Hazel said. "They need people watching. No watchers, no show." She looked at her agenda, all six items, and realized item three had taught her more than items one and two put together. Tomorrow she would write the meeting plan differently, with room for whatever actually happened. "Okay, back to the porch," she said. "We never settled the candy question, and I still have three items left. Bring the chips."

Brody sat on the flat wooden bench behind the baseball diamond, his right arm sweating inside its white cast. Six weeks, the doctor had said, and that was two weeks ago. Across the field, Coach Delgado was running drills, and Brody watched every throw like he could absorb it through his eyes.

His grandfather lowered himself onto the bench beside him with a grunt. Grandpa's left wrist wore a cast too, tan colored and dented at the thumb. "Ten weeks for me," Grandpa said, wiggling his fingers. "You'll beat me out of mine by a month, I'd wager."

Brody frowned. Same kind of break, he knew that much. He had been there in June when Grandpa tripped on the porch step, and three weeks later Brody had landed wrong diving for a line drive, and the x-rays had looked almost identical, side by side on the light board. Same bone, same crack, same doctor. So why ten weeks for Grandpa and six for him?

That was the question he turned over all through batting practice. It was plausible that the doctor just liked kids better, but that seemed weak. It was plausible that Grandpa's break was secretly worse, except the x-rays had matched. Brody liked explanations he could test.

So he tested one. At halftime of his sister's soccer game the next Saturday, he walked the sideline with a notebook and asked every person he could find who had ever broken a bone: how old were you, and how long was the cast on. Marcus, age twelve, five weeks. Marcus's mom, age thirty-eight, nine weeks. The referee had broken his ankle at forty-five and spent three months in a boot. By the end of the afternoon Brody had twelve names, and the pattern jumped right off the page. Every kid was out of a cast faster than every grown-up.

He showed the notebook to his grandfather on Sunday. Grandpa read it slowly, tapped the column of numbers, and laughed. "Young bones heal faster than old ones. Kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." He shook his head. "Sixty-eight years old and learning it from a thirteen-year-old with a notebook."

The day Brody's cast came off, the nurse cut it away with a little buzzing saw and let the sunlight expose his pale, skinny arm to the air for the first time in a month. It looked strange, like it belonged to a younger kid. Outside, Grandpa was waiting in the truck with the window down and the ball bag already loaded.

"Think that arm still works?" Grandpa asked.

Brody rolled down the window the rest of the way, picked up a baseball from the seat, and fired it straight into his grandfather's glove.

The parking lot was already half full when Adam's mom pulled up beside the gym doors, and his heart started hammering before he even touched the door handle. His stomach flipped too, like something small was doing somersaults in there, and he frowned at his own hands because they wouldn't hold still.

"You okay?" his mom asked.

"Fine," Adam said, which was mostly true. He wanted to go in. He'd wanted to go all week, ever since Priya said she'd save him a dance. So why was his body acting like he was about to be chased by wolves?

His best friend Dex came jogging across the lot, holding his phone up like a trophy. "Mr. Holloway let me plug into the speakers for two songs. Two! I'm basically the DJ generator of this whole dance. If those songs go over, he said maybe homecoming."

"That's huge," Adam said, but his stomach flipped again, harder.

Dex squinted at him. "Dude, you look like you're going to throw up on that car."

"I'm not nervous," Adam said. "That's the weird part. I want to be in there." Then he thought about it, turning it over the way he turned over a math problem. His heart was racing. His stomach felt wrong. If it were actual fear, wouldn't he want to leave? But he wanted to stay. So maybe the nervous part came first, even before he felt nervous, and the rest of him was just catching up. He'd read something once about butterflies, and now he tested it out loud: "Maybe it's just butterflies."

"Butterflies," Dex repeated, nodding like a scientist. "Nervousness gives you that. Your heart goes fast and it pulls blood away from your stomach, so it feels like that."

"So if I get my heart to slow down, the butterflies quit?" Adam didn't wait for an answer. He breathed in slow through his nose, out slow through his mouth, four times, while Dex watched with the fascinated horror of someone seeing a friend do something embarrassing in public.

Halfway through the fifth breath, Adam realized his stomach had stopped flipping. His heart still beat fast, but it was the good kind now, the kind that came from the music leaking out under the gym doors and the laughing inside and the fact that in about nine minutes he would be standing in front of Priya.

"Okay," he said, and pulled his jacket tighter even though it was too thin to insulate him from the October cold. "Let's go make you famous."

Dex's grin was infectious. He shoved his phone in his pocket and pushed through the doors first, and Adam followed him straight into the noise and the lights.

Claire kept a systematic list in her notebook titled "What Makes a Story Work," and so far it had three items: dialogue goes in quotation marks, each new speaker gets a new paragraph, and something big has to happen near the end. Today was the read-aloud in Mr. Reyes's room, and she had signed up first.

Her story was about a dog named Biscuit who slipped his leash and ran into the woods behind the school. In her favorite part, the narrator waded through brush and found Biscuit hiding under a log covered with a shelf-like fungus, trembling but safe. She had checked every line of dialogue twice. "Come here, boy," the narrator called. "It's okay." Commas, quotation marks, new paragraphs, all correct. She raised her hand when Mr. Reyes called her name.

She read slowly, saving the best part. When she reached the log, the room got quiet. Marcus, who sat in front and usually drew monsters during read-alouds, had actually put down his pencil. Claire's voice sped up. "The branches snapped back as she knelt. 'Come here, boy,' she called. 'It's okay.' Biscuit crept out and pressed against her legs." She stopped. That was the last line on the page, and it felt like landing a jump off a high wall.

Marcus's hand shot up. "What happened to the dog after that? Did she take him home? Did her mom find out she skipped piano to look for him?" Three other kids nodded. Marcus said, "You can't just stop. I'll boycott sharing day if people keep doing endings like that." A few kids laughed, but Claire's stomach dropped. She had spent all her time on the dialogue and the rescue, and she hadn't noticed that the story quit exactly when the exciting part was over.

She sat down and pulled out her notebook. Mr. Reyes was walking around checking drafts, so she tapped Marcus's shoulder. "You said what happened after. Is there a name for that part?" Marcus shrugged, but Priya behind them held up a checklist from the writing folder and pointed to the last two lines. Claire read them, then read them again. "Falling action and resolution," she said under her breath.

At lunch she added to her list, working through it line by line. After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. Priya's question was still ringing in her ears, so Claire flipped to a clean page and started writing. "They walked home in the dark, Biscuit's leash wound twice around her wrist. Her mom was on the porch, and she was not smiling." Marcus leaned over from the next seat. "Now I want to know what the mom says."

The smell of whiteboard marker hung in the air of Room 12 as Noemie stared at the board. 3x + 4 = 19. She was supposed to do the same thing to both sides, like a scale that had to stay balanced, but the x kept hiding behind the numbers, refusing to show what it was worth.

"How do you know it balances if you can't see inside?" she asked her lab partner, Deshawn.

"You just trust it," he said, tapping his pencil. Deshawn wanted to beat his older brother, who had finished this worksheet in ten minutes flat. He was racing, and racing made him messy.

Noemie tried it anyway. Take 4 from both sides. 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3. She whispered it aloud, feeling the balance of it, and wrote x = 5. She checked by putting 5 back in, and both sides came out 19, like two doors opening onto the same room. Something she couldn't see had been there the whole time, and she had dug it out.

Then came the next problem, and the trouble. Deshawn grabbed the marker and wrote 2x + 3x + 3 = 23. Under it, fast and confident, he scribbled 5x + 3 = 23, then kept going, but before that he had crossed something out. Noemie leaned over. His first line had said 2x + 3 = 5x, treating the lonely 3 as if it belonged with the x's.

"You combined the 3 with the 2x," she said.

"So? They're all smushed together on the same side."

"But they're not the same kind of thing." She picked up a handful of counters from the bin. Two red counters, then three more red counters. "Two x's plus three x's, that's five x's." She set down a single blue counter. "But this 3 is just a 3. You can't squish it in with the x ones. It's like adding apples to a mystery box."

Deshawn frowned at the counters. "The 2x and the 3x are like terms," he said slowly, as if remembering something. He tried combining the 2x and 3x first, leaving the plain 3 alone, then subtracted 3 from both sides and got 5x = 20. "So x is 4." He checked it, and his face split into a grin. He was still going to tell his brother he'd won.

At lunch, Deshawn pushed his tray across the table toward Noemie, offering half a cookie, a small payment that symbolized more than it looked. "My grandma," he said, "she's a retired teacher. I told her about the apples and the mystery box, and she asked me one thing. She asked, 'What does the x stand for?'"

"What did you say?"

"I said, I have no idea, but it's definitely not a 3."

Noemie laughed so abruptly that milk nearly came out of her nose. "Okay, but seriously. What does it stand for?"

Deshawn shrugged and bit into the cookie. "Grandma says that's the whole game. Find out what's hiding."

Natalie had one day left before her grandmother flew in from Monterrey, and so far she could say exactly one full sentence in Spanish: "Tengo un perro pequeño que se llama Biscuit." She said it to the mirror, to the toaster, and to Biscuit himself, who wagged at anything with her voice attached to it. Her mother, who advocated loudly for family bonds whenever Natalie wanted to skip a call, had made her a deal: describe every person and pet in the house in full sentences by tonight, and she could pick the movie on Friday.

She was working on "Mi hermano Marcus tiene quince años y toca la guitarra mal" when Marcus wandered in eating cereal from the box. "You know what's weird," he said. "In French class we just learned you're supposed to say vous to strangers. Like, always. Madame Perrin made us practice it on the janitor and he looked so confused."

Natalie wrote that down, mostly to make him go away. Then she texted her friend Priya, who took German on weekends, and Priya sent back a single message: "Sie. Same thing. My teacher says you'd sound like a toddler without it." So French had vous, German had Sie, and Natalie had a suspicion her Spanish book was hiding the same rule somewhere. The book only said usted meant "you," which was spectacularly unhelpful, since tú also meant "you." Two words, one meaning, no explanation. There had to be a pattern, and nobody was going to hand it to her.

The doorbell rang before she could stew on it. On the porch stood a small older woman in a raincoat, holding a handwritten address that had clearly survived a washing machine. "Busco Maple Street," she said. "Perdón, ¿dónde queda?"

Here it was: a stranger, a real one, asking directions, and Natalie's mouth was already loading the familiar tú she used with Marcus and Biscuit. She caught it mid-launch. Testing time. "Queda a dos cuadras, señora," Natalie said. "¿Usted busca la casa azul?" The woman's whole face did something warm and unhurried, like a cat settling into sun. She talked for a full minute about her granddaughter, the weather in Guadalajara, and the terrible numbering on Maple Street, and Natalie understood maybe half of it and nodded at all the right gaps. When she left, the woman squeezed her arm and said, "Qué niña tan educada."

Natalie closed the door and stood there feeling extremely spontaneous, in a planned and rehearsed sort of way. Then she went back to the kitchen, erased half her sentence list, and rewrote every line for her grandmother in the usted form, out loud, while Biscuit supervised from the warm spot by the fridge. "Mi abuela llega mañana," she told him. "Ella es la persona más terca que yo conozco." Biscuit yawned. From the hallway, Marcus called, "Was that Spanish or did you hurt yourself?"

"Usted no entiende nada," she called back.

Theo had been looking forward to Marcus's birthday sleepover for three weeks, and then Marcus's elbow knocked Theo's slice of pizza straight off the table and onto the carpet. "Nice one," Theo said, loud enough for everyone to hear. Marcus laughed with the other guys, and Theo decided, right there, that it was on purpose. Marcus had been showing off all night, taking the good controller, hogging the VR headset. This was just the newest move.

He spent the next hour collecting evidence. When Marcus passed the popcorn bowl past him to Dev, that was a snub. When Marcus picked Theo last for the Halo team, that was an insult. Theo's awareness of every little slight felt acute, like a radio tuned to one station: everything Marcus did, Marcus did to him.

At two in the morning, the guys were asleep and Theo was still awake, staring at the glow-in-the-dark stars on Marcus's ceiling. He started to replay the pizza moment, frame by frame, like rewinding a video. Marcus had been reaching across for the garlic knots. His chair legs had squeaked sideways just before his elbow moved. Had Marcus even been looking at Theo? He hadn't. His eyes were on the food. Theo sat up. Maybe he had tested the wrong theory the whole night. His simple idea: rerun each "insult" and ask one question, was there another possible cause? Popcorn bowl: it was on Dev's side. Halo teams: Marcus was balancing skill levels, and Theo actually stunk at Halo. Every clue had a second explanation.

At breakfast, Theo watched Marcus get up for juice, and Marcus's sneaker skidded on a patch of floor near the counter. "Whoa," Marcus said, arms windmilling, and Theo noticed a faint slick spot, probably from the pizza grease tracked off the carpet the night before. It was two feet from the table. Right where a chair pushing back could lose its grip.

"Marcus," Theo said. "Last night. The pizza. Did you slip?"

Marcus set the juice down. "Dude, yeah. My chair totally skated on something. I was going for the knots. Why, you thought I did it on purpose?"

"Maybe," Theo admitted. "Everything you did all night seemed aimed at me. I kept assuming you meant it."

"That's called hostile attribution bias," Marcus said, grinning. "My sister says I have it about my math teacher."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly choked on his waffles. "Okay, but in my defense, you were being annoying about the headset."

"I'll share the headset," Marcus said, sliding the last waffle onto Theo's plate. "Frontier day, my turn to explore new planets. You call shotgun on the goggles."

"Deal," said Theo, and grabbed the syrup.

"Delete it," Marcus said, hovering over Nicholas's shoulder. "Delete the whole group chat before Mr. Herrera sees it."

On the screen, the new class chat was already on fire. Someone had posted forty-seven crying-laughing emojis about Mr. Herrera's mustard-stained tie, someone else had replied in ALL CAPS, and Danny had nominated himself "Supreme Chat Overlord" in a message that scrolled for three paragraphs. Nicholas scrolled slowly, like a person watching a nature documentary. "Did you notice how everyone writes differently in here than they do out loud? Danny whisper-talks in class. In the chat he's basically shouting."

Marcus groaned and dropped onto the beanbag. "That's not the problem. The problem is Mr. Herrera made the chat for the volcano project, and now it's a volcano."

Nicholas kept scrolling, and a question started forming, the kind that itched. Had anyone ever written actual rules for this? Not school rules, but manners, the online kind? He typed it into the search bar while Marcus built a sandwich of suspense, saying nothing, just raising one eyebrow and waiting.

The results loaded. Nicholas blinked. "Okay, this is real. Somebody did write it down. It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines,' and it was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC?" Marcus peered at the phone, a chip halfway to his mouth. "That sounds like a robot's gym locker."

"Probably some official document thing," Nicholas said, scrolling. The old text talked about not shouting in capitals, thinking before you post, remembering a real human reads your words. It was written before group chats even existed, back when phones had cords, and yet it described Danny exactly. Nicholas laughed out loud. "This guy predicted Danny in 1995. That's twenty years before Danny."

"So what do we do, print it and tape it to his locker?"

Nicholas was already typing, borrowing the old rules and rewriting them in Danny's own language. He posted: "Chat Constitution, Article 1: no caps unless spontaneous genuine screaming. Article 2: three emojis maximum. Article 3: volcanoes only."

The chat went quiet. Then Danny appeared in the doorway of Marcus's kitchen, still holding his phone, wearing the expression of a Supreme Chat Overlord who had just discovered he could be overthrown. "Article 2 is tyranny," he said. "I demand a rewrite."

"Nominate yourself to the rules committee," Nicholas said, and held up the phone so Danny could see the yellowed 1995 document on the screen. Danny leaned in, squinted, and read the title twice.

"Wait," he said. "They had internet manners before I was born and nobody told me?"

Max stood in front of a painting of a narrow street at the city gallery, his sketchbook clamped under one arm, scowling. His homework was to draw a street using one-point perspective, where every line ran toward a single vanishing point, and his version at home looked like a street designed by a dizzy giant. He had a letter from his art teacher folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out and read it again. "Max," it said, "go find the museum's oldest street painting. Find the point where the buildings' edges would meet if you extended them with a ruler. Then look at the round things. The lamp, the fruit cart, the boy's ball. If a sphere is shaded, the highlight is the brightest spot, and it sits on the side facing the light. Its position shows you where the light is coming from. Copy that, and your street will stop looking flat."

The painting, he discovered, was in a room with a skylight, and it did have a fruit cart with an orange on it. Max found the vanishing point first, tracing the building edges with his pencil in the air until they all aimed at a spot on the far door of the street, like the whole town was sliding toward it. Then he looked at the orange. It had one bright dab of paint on its upper left side, brighter than anything else on it. He held up his pencil as a pretend lamp, imagining the light arriving from exactly there, and checked a marble on the cobblestones nearby. Brightest spot, upper left. The cart wheel's rim caught its shine on the upper left too. It was a rule hiding under the paint, invisible until you hunted for it, and now Max saw little spotlight dots everywhere, like the street was secretly lit by a guild of tiny invisible lamplighters, all standing in the same corner of the sky.

"Excuse me," said a girl beside him, maybe ten, holding her own sketchbook open to a gray circle that looked like a flat gray cookie. "Mine's supposed to be a sphere but it looks like a blob. The docent said I should shade it, but I don't know where."

"Which side is the lamp on?" Max asked. He had decided to pretend he was a gallery wizard, since the skylight made everything glow anyway. "A sphere's highlight is the brightest spot, and it's on the side facing the light. So pick where your lamp is, and put your brightest spot there."

The girl bit her lip, jabbed a finger at the upper right of her circle, and drew one small brilliant dot. The blob popped into a ball so suddenly that she laughed out loud, and a guard three rooms away said "Shh" with impressive authority for someone so far away.

Max sat down on the gallery bench and started a fresh street. This time he drew the vanishing point first, aimed every roofline at it like roads to a castle, and gave each round thing, a lamp, a barrel, a bicycle bell, its brightest spot on the upper left, so that his whole imaginary street was lit by the same invisible sun. He was halfway through when the girl leaned over and said, "Your street looks nutritious enough to eat," and Max, who had been thinking of it as a place, had to admit that a street you could eat was even better, so he added a bakery with round golden loaves in the window, each with one bright spot, upper left, shining.

The group chat had forty-seven messages by the time Simon sat down with his toast. It was the chat for the science fair, the one Mr. Okafor had set up, and someone had posted a photo of Maya's volcano display. Under it, from Priya's account, was a single line: "this looks like it was made by a third grader."

Simon read it twice. Priya was the girl who said "excuse me" to doors. She had lent him a pencil on Tuesday and thanked him for returning it as if he had done her a favor. He scrolled up and found three more sharp comments from her that week, each one public, each one aimed at somebody's project. In the hallway that same week she had complimented Maya's poster to her face. Simon had heard it himself.

He typed "why are you being so mean?" and then deleted it, because forty people would read it, and a public fight would just transport the whole mess somewhere worse. Instead he started a private chat. His assumption was that Priya would deny it, so he tested it with something small first. "Hey, was that you on the volcano comment?"

"obviously," she wrote back. "it's true. she glued the lava on crooked."

"Do you tell her that in person?"

There was a long pause, long enough for Simon to eat half his toast. Then: "no. that would be rude."

"Ruder than typing it?"

"typing doesn't count," Priya wrote, and Simon could almost see her shrug. He stared at the screen. It did count, though. The words were the same words; only the room was different.

He searched "why are people meaner online" and the first result was about something a psychologist named John Suler had described in 2004, called the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Simon read it twice. That was it, exactly, Priya in one sentence. He pasted the link into the private chat.

A minute passed. Then Priya sent a single defiant "so???" followed by, "ok fine maybe the volcano comment was too much." In the main group chat, a new message appeared from her account: "hey Maya, the lava on your volcano is actually straighter than I said. sorry. also I found out my brain is broken in a normal way, ask Simon for the link."

Maya replied with a photo of her volcano wearing a tiny paper crown, and the caption "the third grader accepts your apology."

Christopher carried the folding chairs two at a time across the grass, because if he made three trips instead of five, he could get back to the pavilion before Aunt Ruth finished arranging the Seder plates. His family had claimed the corner of the park with the big oak trees, and long tables stretched under the branches where the Seder would happen, the whole meal that told the story of the Jews leaving Egypt, escaping from slavery under the pharaoh. "That pharaoh was like the worst landlord in history," Uncle Danny had joked that morning. "Wouldn't let his workers go no matter what." Christopher had laughed, then wondered what it would feel like to work for someone like that.

The real problem was Zoe. His cousin was seven, the youngest able child at the table, and all week she had been practicing the Four Questions on index cards she kept losing. She practiced them in the car, at breakfast, even once into the bathroom mirror while Christopher waited outside the door. At the Seder, the youngest one asks the Four Questions, and Zoe had whispered to him, "What if I freeze and everybody stares?"

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before the meal started. His theory was that Zoe froze only when she felt alone, like the time she forgot her line at the school play. If she had someone to aim her words at, just one face instead of forty, maybe the words would come out fine. So while the grown-ups poured grape juice and set out the parsley and salt water, Christopher pulled two chairs behind the oak tree.

"Practice on me," he said. "Pretend everyone else is furniture."

Zoe narrowed her eyes at him. "Furniture doesn't eat karpas."

"Fine, very hungry furniture." She laughed, and then she asked him the first question, her voice wobbly at first, about how this night was different from all other nights. He noticed something: her hands stopped shaking when he nodded along, and by the third question she was looking straight at him, steady as a held note.

When the time came, the gradual fading of the afternoon light made the park smell like cut grass and someone's charcoal grill nearby. Aunt Ruth tapped her glass. Zoe stood up, and Christopher watched her scan the tables, watched panic flicker across her face, and then he caught her eye and gave one small nod, the exact nod from behind the oak tree. She took a breath, turned toward everyone, and asked all Four Questions without stopping once, her voice carrying past the tables toward the playground where kids on the swings went quiet to listen.

Afterward, Grandma Miriam squeezed Zoe's shoulder and said, "Some years these questions make me cry." Christopher bit into his matzah, which crumbled all over his shirt, and thought about how a person could grow like the oak overhead, thriving in good soil. Then Zoe plopped down beside him and whispered, "Same time next year?"

"Only if I'm still furniture," he whispered back.

Laurence set her easel on the grass beside her cousin Dev, who had decided that anyone could paint a portrait in one afternoon. She had her grandmother's old box of watercolours, the pan nearly gone in the yellow corner, and a photograph of her grandmother propped against the fence. "You don't just draw it once," she said. "You start with the palest wash and let it dry, then add darker ones. Light to dark. You can't go backwards."

Dev frowned at his paper. He was more interested in the fence behind his drawing of the shed, and he had pressed so hard with his pencil that every guide line had carved a groove. "I'll just erase these later," he said.

Laurence remembered last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while her mother winced over a drawing of the living room. Her mother had pressed hard too, back when she was learning, and no eraser had lifted the lines. The finished room had stayed covered in them, faint rails running across the ceiling and floor, because the guide lines for perspective are drawn lightly with a hard pencil so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in. Her mother had said, "You have to trust that the lines are there even when you can barely see them." Laurence had thought that was strange advice for drawing, and stranger still for everything else.

She laid her first wash, the palest peach, over the whole face and let the sun do the drying. While she waited she watched Dev scrub at his paper with the eraser until it pilled and tore. The grooves stayed. He flipped his board over, and she noticed the lines showed through the back, like bones under skin. "Try drawing the fence again on a fresh sheet," she said, "but press like you're drawing on a soap bubble."

Dev gave her the look he saved for advice from girls, the stereotype that art was her side of the family, some hereditary thing that had skipped him. But he picked up the hard 4H pencil she handed him and drew so lightly he had to tilt the sheet to see his own lines. "That's not drawing," he complained. "That's whispering."

"That's how it's supposed to look," Laurence said. She touched her brush to the second wash, a deeper rose along the jaw, and watched the first layer glow up through it. Dev leaned over her shoulder, holding his whispery fence up beside it.

"Okay," he said. "Teach me the faces next."

The lights went out at 8:40, right in the middle of Brooklyn's game, and the screen died to black. Her little brother Theo groaned from the couch. Their mom found the candles in the kitchen drawer, the ones shaped like pinecones that smelled like a fake forest, and set three of them on the coffee table. The flames leaned sideways whenever anyone walked past, throwing wobbly shadows up the wall.

"I was about to beat the whole level," Theo said.

"Beat it tomorrow." Brooklyn stared at the dark television. Then she remembered something her cousin Dev had told her last summer, after a storm knocked out power across his whole network of streets. He had lost his desktop computer that night. When the electricity came back on, he said, a surge of power had shot through the house and fried the machine. Emergency agencies told people to unplug their computers and other electronics during a power cut, because when the power returned, the surge could damage them.

"I didn't believe him at first," she said out loud, crouching behind the TV. "I thought he spilled juice on it and made up the surge thing." She pulled the console's plug from the wall and coiled the cord around her hand. Next she went to the desk in the corner and unplugged the desktop computer, then the router blinking dark on the shelf, then the microwave in the kitchen. Theo followed her with a candle, dripping wax onto a plate he carried like a waiter.

"What if the power comes back on while you're asleep?" he asked.

"That's the point. It can come back any time, and everything plugged in gets hit." She pointed at the lamp by the couch. "That one too, please."

The power stayed off until after 10. They played shadow puppets on the ceiling, and Theo made a shape he claimed was an authentic wolf, though it looked more like a rabbit with big ears. Brooklyn drew a map of the neighborhood in her notebook, trying to depict which streets might be dark, guessing it was just their block since the kitchen window showed lights glowing two houses down.

At 10:20 the ceiling fan spun once, the lamps blazed on, and the refrigerator started humming in the kitchen. The television screen stayed black and quiet, its plug lying on the floor where Brooklyn had left it. She smiled at it, then went around the room picking up her candles.

"Tomorrow, level twelve," Theo said. "Nobody fried."

"Nobody fried," Brooklyn said, and blew out the last pinecone.

The bleachers smelled like hot dogs and cut grass, and Violet's whole family had claimed the middle rows for the championship game between the Riverside Rockets and the Northside Bears. Her uncle Marco was already hoarse from yelling, and the game had not even started. "The crowd wins games," he kept shouting, drumming his fists on the railing. "That's the whole point of home field!" Violet frowned. She wanted the Rockets to win, and she wanted to believe Uncle Marco, but something about his claim bugged her, like a math problem with a step missing.

She thought back to two winters ago, when she had watched football at her grandmother's apartment during the year of the empty stadiums. The TV had shown rows and rows of vacant seats, and the games had felt strange and quiet, like a forest with no birds. Grandma had read the season totals out loud from her newspaper at the time, and the numbers had stuck in Violet's head ever since. She pulled out her phone now and searched until she found the page again, just to be sure.

"Uncle Marco," she said, tugging his sleeve during a timeout. "You know the season when almost nobody was allowed in the stadiums? Home teams finished 127 wins, 128 losses, and one tie. There was basically no home advantage at all." Marco blinked at her. Her cousin Jayden leaned over. "Wait, so cheering does nothing?" Violet shrugged. "It did nothing that year, at least. Maybe it's something else about home field. Maybe it's the players, not us." Marco looked wounded, like she had told him his cooking was bad. "Fine, science girl," he said. "Test it. Next few plays, nobody cheers. Then everybody goes wild. See what happens."

Violet felt a little thrill. An experiment, right here in the bleachers. She asked the families around them, and even a man with a foam finger agreed to stay silent for the next three plays. The stadium went oddly quiet, and the Rockets gave up a sack. Then she raised both arms, and the whole section erupted. The next play, the Bears intercepted the ball anyway. Marco threw up his hands. "That proves nothing!" Jayden laughed. "You need way more plays than that. That's the point, isn't it? One moment can't tell you anything." Violet nodded. Three plays was noise, not a pattern.

So they kept going, quiet then loud, loud then quiet, marking each result in her notebook, and by the fourth quarter she had a messy little chart that proved absolutely nothing except that the Rockets were aggressive on defense no matter what the crowd did. When the final interception sealed the win, Marco swept her up in a hug anyway. "All right," he admitted. "Maybe the cheering is for us." Violet grinned and waved her notebook above her head like a trophy. "Best data I ever salvaged from a blowout," she said, and Jayden said, "Save me a seat for the rematch."

Kayla laced her sneakers at the kitchen table while her mom buttered toast, because today was her first day volunteering at the River Street Food Bank. "Remember when you were six," her mom said, "and you cried because we threw out the jack-o'-lantern?" Kayla laughed. She had wanted to keep it on the porch forever, and when it softened and collapsed, she had buried it under the maple tree with a popsicle-stick marker. She still couldn't stand seeing food thrown away, which was exactly why she had signed up to volunteer.

The food bank smelled like cardboard and oranges. A supervisor named Dara handed Kayla a box of donated groceries from Hartman's Market: lettuce with brown edges, apples with dents, peppers that had gone soft in spots. "Sort the good from the not good," Dara said. "Blemished is fine. Rotten is not."

Kayla worked down the row, but a question kept nagging her. These vegetables weren't rotten, they were just ugly or slightly old, and the store had gotten rid of them anyway. She counted the box quickly: forty-two items, and thirty-one were still perfectly good if you cut around the spots. That was more than half saved from the trash. She wondered how big that number would get if you counted every store, every kitchen, every school cafeteria in the whole country.

She found Dara stacking cans. "Do you know how much food in the whole United States just gets wasted, never eaten?" Dara smiled. "Actually, yes. The Department of Agriculture estimates between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." Kayla stared. Out of every ten boxes like this one, three or four never fed anybody at all.

She wanted to test it. At home that afternoon, she pulled everything out of her own refrigerator and counted: sixty items. If the estimate held for her family too, somewhere between eighteen and twenty-four of them would end up in the garbage. She made a plan, writing it on the whiteboard by the fridge. Leftover rice became fried rice. Soft apples became applesauce. The half-onion went into soup. By the end of the week the trash can was nearly empty, and her little brother, Marcus, who usually complained about leftovers, asked for seconds of the applesauce and said it tasted better than the store kind, almost like something from the artisan bakery downtown, the way the whole house smelled like cinnamon.

At her next shift, Kayla told Dara about the experiment, and Dara gave her a new job: teaching the sorting table to keep slightly blemished fruit out of the discard bin. "You have a distinct talent for this," Dara said, handing her a permanent marker to label the rescue crate. Kayla wrote RESCUED on the side in big letters, then set a rescued apple on top, where everybody could see it.

Owen set his pencil down and glared at the paper. His street looked like a street that had been through a landslide. The buildings on the left leaned one way, the buildings on the right leaned the other, and the road between them wandered off the page like a snake that had lost its glasses. He wanted to draw the view from his grandmother's front porch, the one she said she might have to sell, so he could give her the picture before the moving truck came. He had one week.

"You're frowning at that paper like it insulted you," his mom said, setting a lemon on the counter. She turned it over, squinted, and muttered, "Is that fungus? I think that's fungus." She dropped the whole thing in the trash and came to stand behind him.

"Perspective," Owen said. "You're supposed to make lines go to a vanishing point, and I get that, but my street won't cooperate."

His mom pulled out the chair across from him. "Did I ever tell you about the nail hole? In the Last Supper?" She waited while he shook his head. "The single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there."

Owen looked up. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings in the world? You can still see it?"

"Still there."

He sat with that for a second. Strings, from a nail. Strings that stretched out from one spot to guide the lines. So Leonardo hadn't just eyeballed it, and he hadn't started with the walls or the ceiling either. He had started with the one point, the point at Christ's head, and let every line grow outward from there like spokes on a wheel.

Owen flipped to a fresh page. This time he drew nothing but a small dot first, halfway up the paper, right where the street should disappear. He pressed the pencil tip so hard it nearly poked through, then found a thumbtack in the junk drawer, set it exactly on the dot, and looped a piece of sewing thread around it. He pulled the thread taut and drew along its edge, then moved it and drew again, line after line radiating out from the tack like rays from a tiny sun.

"Why the actual thread?" his mom asked.

"Because my hand curves. The thread doesn't."

When the lines were done he took the tack away and built the street on top of them, storefronts, windows, a mailbox. The buildings stood up straight and tall. The road ran true and narrow and went exactly where it was supposed to go, shrinking toward the dot until it vanished. In the middle of the road, far down where everything converged, the paper held one small, dark pinprick where the tack had been.

Owen leaned close to it. "I'm leaving it," he said. "Grandma can find it."

Aiden carried two paper cups of punch across the community hall, scanning the folding tables for his grandmother's church group. The hall had been split in half for the interfaith evening, with hymnbooks on one side and a cloth-covered table on the other, where a Sikh family was arranging a small stand wrapped in saffron fabric. Aiden's assignment for school was due Monday: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had planned to just look things up online, but his grandmother had said the community hall evening would demonstrate more than any website could.

At the Sikh table, a boy about his own age sat copying something into a notebook in careful Punjabi letters. His name tag read Vikram. When Aiden set a cup of punch down beside him, Vikram grinned and covered his page. "You can look. It's not secret." The page was covered with lines of Gurmukhi script, the same lines over and over.

"That's a lot of copying," Aiden said.

"It's Japji Sahib. The morning prayer." Vikram tapped the notebook. "I have to know it well, because I'm getting ready for my initiation."

Aiden frowned. "Like a ceremony?"

"It's called Amrit Sanchar," Vikram said, and then his little sister tugged his sleeve and he went to help her with her shoes, leaving Aiden staring at the notebook.

Aiden wandered back to the church side, where his grandmother was stacking chairs. She had retired from the post office last spring, and now that she drew a pension, she volunteered at events like this almost every weekend. Aiden asked her what she thought happened after death, and she said what she always said, about heaven and being with God. Then she asked what the family across the hall believed.

"I don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "They said something about the soul merging with God, like a drop going back into the ocean. But I got interrupted."

He remembered then, suddenly, a funeral he had attended two years before, for his grandfather. After the service, in the church basement, a man had stood up and described reincarnation so vividly that several of the mourners had leaned forward, listening to something completely different from the minister's sermon. Aiden had been eleven and had thought the man was simply wrong. Now he wondered whether he had been biased that day, hearing only what he already expected to hear.

He marched back across the hall, punch sloshing. "Vikram. For my project. Does Japji Sahib say anything about what happens after you die?"

Vikram's mother looked up from the cloth-covered table and smiled. "Ask him what he's reciting it for," she said, and went back to smoothing the fabric.

"I'm reciting it because it's part of the ceremony," Vikram said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "And the prayer talks about the soul's journey. So I guess learning it is like practicing for the whole thing, the life after this one too." He looked surprised at his own sentence, then pleased.

Aiden wrote fast, filling half a page. "Can I ask you one more thing on Monday? After you've thought about it more?"

"Bring two cups of punch," Vikram said, and turned back to his notebook, pencil moving through the letters one more careful line at a time.

Lea had exactly one job at the polling station: hold the "Vote Here" sign without whacking anyone with it. She was failing. The sign was nearly as tall as she was, and every time a voter walked past, the cardboard corner lunged at somebody's hat.

"I saw that," said Marcus, her best friend, who was supposed to be handing out sample ballots. "Your sign is attacking Mrs. Okafor. Again."

"The sign has a mind of its own. I'm just the camouflage, hiding its sinister plans." Lea wrestled the cardboard into a corner and propped it against the wall like a sleeping dragon.

Their civics class had sent them here to participate in Election Day, which mostly meant standing in the hallway of the community center for two hours. Their teacher, Ms. Reyes, had assigned a worksheet that Lea had stuffed in her back pocket: Read a right listed in the Constitution, then explain it in your own words. She'd been avoiding it all morning.

"Did you do the worksheet?" she asked Marcus.

"I wrote that the Constitution is a big paper that tells the government what it can't do. Very inspiring. Ten out of ten."

Before Lea could argue, a man with a clipboard hurried over. He was from the local newspaper, and he was upset. "They moved me to the parking lot," he said to the poll manager. "I need to photograph inside."

"Rules are rules," the manager said. "No cameras past this line."

Lea watched the man retreat, muttering. Something nagged at her, a pattern she couldn't quite see yet. Marcus had said the Constitution tells the government what it can't do. So what stopped the government from shutting down a newspaper entirely?

She pulled out her phone and searched. The First Amendment. She read it twice, lips moving. It protected freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Five things, all in one amendment. The press. There it was, printed plain as a cereal box label.

"Marcus," she said, yanking his sleeve. "The First Amendment protects the press. And speech. And religion. And peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. That's why that reporter gets to be annoying at all."

"So the government can't just squish newspapers?"

"Apparently not." Lea flipped her worksheet over and wrote fast, in her own words: The First Amendment means the government can't tell people what to believe, what to say, or what to print, and it can't stop us from gathering peacefully or complaining to its face.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Complaining to its face. Truly your finest work."

The reporter came back through the doors, camera bouncing on his chest, having negotiated a spot near the door. He raised the camera toward the check-in table, and Lea, without thinking, yanked her sign out of the corner to hold it high and proud.

The cardboard corner clipped his clipboard, and his pen flew across the floor.

"You're attacking the press now," Marcus said. "The exact press we just learned is protected."

Lea chased the pen, held it out to the reporter, and grinned. "Freedom of the press," she said. "And freedom of my sign. Somebody should write an amendment about that one."

At the first turn of the track, Madison bent to retie her shoe even though it didn't need it, because bending gave her an excuse not to look at the girl stretching beside her. That girl was Priya, the fastest eighth grader in the county, and in twenty minutes they would both toe the line for the eight hundred metres, the race Madison had bombed at twice already.

"You went out too fast last time," Priya said, not unkindly. "I watched. First lap like a rocket, second lap like a walk."

"I know," Madison said. The embarrassment still stung from the meet where she'd led at four hundred metres and then been passed by six people, one by one, her legs turning to wet cardboard. The trouble was she couldn't feel it happening. Everything seemed fine until suddenly it wasn't, which meant the problem was hidden somewhere she couldn't see, in the way she spent her energy, like a bank account draining without receipts.

Her brother Dev, who swam, had run into a version of the same puzzle last summer. "Freestyle," he'd told her, frowning at the television. "You'd think everyone would pick something different, right? Like, it's free. Any stroke you want."

"So why doesn't anyone?"

"I asked my coach. Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races, because it's the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes. It's just faster. That's the whole answer." Dev had shrugged. "But you still have to swim it smart, because if you go out too hard, even front crawl won't save you."

Madison had rolled her eyes at the time. Now, standing at the line under an ominous gray sky, the idea came back to her from a new angle. The swimmers didn't win by choosing the fastest stroke alone; they won by managing the fastest stroke. Maybe pace worked the same way. The first lap of an eight hundred wasn't the race at all. It was an investment, and if she poured everything into it, there'd be nothing left when the actual race began.

So she made a plan she could test: on the first lap she would stay three steps behind Priya, no closer, no matter how easy it felt. If the plan was wrong, she'd lose again and know it. If it was right, the second lap would tell her.

The gun cracked. Priya swept to the front, and Madison sat three steps back, her legs begging to go, the whole field stringing out behind them. Four hundred metres. The bell. Then, coming off the final turn, the gap ahead of her began to shrink, one step at a time, like the second half of a race she'd never actually run before. She surged. Twenty metres out she was even with Priya's shoulder, hearing her own breath like a drum.

"Where did you come from?" Priya gasped.

Madison didn't waste the air to answer. She just leaned forward and ran through the line.

Aiden opened the group chat for the Science Olympiad team at 7:03 p.m. and found forty-one unread messages, which was never good. The facts, as far as he could piece together from the wall of text, were these: Marcus had left his weather station project at home, Priya had told Mr. Okafor that the missing data had been collected when it hadn't, and she'd done it because Marcus had covered for her little brother the week before when the brother got caught sneaking into the gym. Everyone agreed on all of it. Nobody agreed on anything else.

"she LIED to a teacher," Devon typed. "the rest of the team worked hard on real data and she faked ours. that's a fairness thing. rules apply to everyone or they apply to no one."

"she was paying back a debt," Zoe answered. "Marcus protected her brother. you don't drop people who helped you. that's loyalty, devon, look it up."

Aiden read it twice. That was the strange part. Devon and Zoe weren't fighting about what had happened. They were fighting about what it meant, using the exact same forty-one messages as evidence. He thought about how light bends through a prism and comes out in different directions depending on the glass, how the same beam refracts into colors that weren't visible before. Same light in, different light out. He had a hypothesis: the facts weren't the problem at all. He decided to test it.

He typed: "devon, name one fact you and zoe disagree about. an actual fact."

The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in this group was like a year. Then Devon wrote, "okay. none. she did it, marcus owed her, okafor believed her. we agree."

"so you agree on every single fact," Aiden typed, "and you still land on opposite sides."

"yes???" Zoe sent, followed by the confused emoji and then, "oh."

Aiden's mom knocked on his door and said something about the weather forecast, precipitation moving in overnight, did he have his rain jacket by the door. "Yeah, in a minute," he said, because something was happening in the chat. Devon had sent a screenshot of the team rulebook, and Zoe had sent a photo of the poster in the gym that said WE TAKE CARE OF OUR OWN, and they were now arguing about which document mattered more, which was, Aiden realized, the same argument wearing a new shirt.

He tried one more test. "imagine priya covered for someone who was NOT her friend. devon, would you be madder or less mad?"

"same," Devon said.

"same," Zoe said, "but because it would be pointless loyalty."

Aiden laughed out loud, alone in his room, at two people typing "same" about opposite feelings. He typed, "wait. you both just said priya values something different than you do. devon you value fairness. zoe you value loyalty. nobody's wrong about the facts. you're not even wrong about the values. you just have different ones."

There was a long pause. Then Marcus, silent for the entire fight, finally appeared.

"guys. I'm quitting the team either way. I don't want priya taking heat for me," he wrote. "also aiden you type like a documentary narrator but you're right."

Zoe sent, "we could split into two teams. one for fairness, one for loyalty."

Devon sent, "that's the dumbest idea I've ever heard. I love it."

Aiden looked at the rain starting against his window and went to get his jacket, and when he came back there was a new chat, created by Zoe, named Team Loyalty, and another one already created by Devon, named Team Fairness, and both of them had added him at the same time.

Amelia slid her copy of To Kill a Mockingbird across the library table so the worn cover faced the circle of folding chairs. It was her turn to lead book club, and she had drafted her notes on three index cards, which now stuck together in her nervous hands. She peeled them apart and cleared her throat.

"Okay, so, symbolism," she began. "My cards say a symbol is when an object stands for a bigger idea, but I want to try something instead of just reading that. Everybody, think about the title. Why mockingbirds?"

Dev, who had eaten half a cookie already, raised his hand even though nobody needed to. "Because they're in the book? Atticus says something about them."
